exploreAction.instruction: The monk is a speck — you may need to search for him. The sky and sea are almost the same tone, a wall of silence. Kleist said looking at it felt like having your eyelids cut off: you are alone with the infinite.

name: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus (1560)
teaser: Bruegel's Icarus splashes into the sea in the corner while a farmer plows, a shepherd stares at the sky, and a ship sails on — nobody stops. It may not even be Bruegel, and it is the most famous depiction of indifference in art.

exploreAction.targetName: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus (1560) by Bruegel, Musées Royaux Brussels
exploreAction.instruction: Look for Icarus: just two white legs kicking in the water beside the ship. The plowman works on; the sun shines; the world does not stop for the boy who flew too high. The poem by W.H. Auden — 'About suffering they were never wrong, the Old Masters' — is about this exact painting.

name: The Massacre of the Innocents (1567)
teaser: Bruegel's soldiers enter a Flemish village to seize children from mothers — painted as a biblical scene but read as a Spanish atrocity in the Netherlands. The horror is in the everyday setting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Massacre of the Innocents (1567) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The soldiers are not monsters — they are soldiers doing a job in a winter village. Mothers struggle, a horse rears, snow falls. Bruegel set a massacre in a place that looks like home, and that is what makes it unbearable.

name: The Blind Leading the Blind (1568)
teaser: Bruegel's line of six blind men follows their leader into a ditch — each already at a different stage of falling. It illustrates a Bible verse and the human condition at once.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blind Leading the Blind (1568) by Bruegel, Museo di Capodimonte
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the chain of falls: the first man is already down, the second is mid-fall, the third is stumbling, the last still walking upright. Bruegel painted each stage of disaster. The church steeple in the background is the destination they will never reach.

name: The Harvesters (1565)
teaser: Bruegel's wheat field at harvest — workers cut the grain, one drinks from a jug, others swim and nap in the shade. It is a summer so real you can almost feel the heat.

exploreAction.targetName: The Harvesters (1565) by Bruegel, Metropolitan Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The wheat field makes a diagonal wall of gold, and beyond it the land falls away to the sea. The workers rest, eat, swim — Bruegel painted work and its breaks as equally real. It is one panel of the lost series of the months, and the only one that survived complete.

name: The Tower of Babel — the small version (1563)
teaser: Bruegel painted the Tower twice — a large version in Vienna and this smaller one in Rotterdam. Both show the same ambition: a spiral city climbing toward a god that will not be reached.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tower of Babel — small version (1563) by Bruegel, Museum Boijmans
exploreAction.instruction: The tower's spiral ramps wind up into cloud — and the top is unfinished, already collapsing into mud and brick. The arched construction recalls the Colosseum; the message is the same as in the Vienna version: every empire builds its own ruin.

name: The Peasant Dance (1568)
teaser: Bruegel's village square erupts into dance — a bagpiper, a kissing couple, children, a table of drinkers. Nobody is painted as noble; everybody is painted as real.

exploreAction.targetName: The Peasant Dance (1568) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The dancers move in a diagonal out of the painting — the piper leads, the couple in the center turns, the table tilts with drink. Bruegel painted the energy of a day off: loud, clumsy, and alive. The church looms behind; the dance is the sermon.

name: The Triumph of Death (1562)
teaser: Bruegel's armies of skeletons sweep across a landscape of burning houses, broken carts, and every rank of humanity — a painting of the plague years that still functions as the definitive memento mori.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of Death (1562) by Bruegel, Prado
exploreAction.instruction: There is no center — death arrives from every side. A knight falls, a king is dragged from his throne, a musician plays on as the skeletons dance. Bruegel painted this during Europe's plague and war years; it is a mass grave with a frame.

name: Netherlandish Proverbs (1559)
teaser: Bruegel's village is a catalogue of over a hundred Dutch proverbs made literal — someone bangs his head against a brick wall, another sows seeds on the wind, a third has a roof of tiles missing from his head.

exploreAction.targetName: Netherlandish Proverbs (1559) by Bruegel, Gemäldegalerie Berlin
exploreAction.instruction: Treat it like a word-search: try to find 'armed to the teeth' (a man with a knife between his teeth), 'the world turned upside down' (a globe with a cross on top), 'to swim against the stream.' There are more than a hundred sayings hidden in the village.

name: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent (1559)
teaser: Bruegel's town square splits down the middle — Carnival's fat man jousts with a kitchen ladle against Lent's thin woman with a baker's peel. Gluttony and fasting face off while the town carries on.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent (1559) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: Carnival, on the left, sits on a wine barrel with a roast pig at his feet; Lent, on the right, pulls a cart of fish and pretzels. The town between them is full of people being both. Bruegel painted the calendar as a perpetual argument between appetite and discipline.

name: The Wedding Dance in the Open Air (1566)
teaser: Bruegel's wedding party dances in a field — couples spinning, a bagpiper, a man trying to kiss a woman who is having none of it. Marriage as a loud, sweaty, joyful fact.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wedding Dance in the Open Air (1566) by Bruegel, Detroit Institute of Arts
exploreAction.instruction: Find the couple in the center mid-spin, and the woman in front of them laughing as her partner pulls her. The dancers' feet are off the ground — Bruegel painted motion so well the painting seems to sway. It is a portrait of a community at its most alive.

name: The Return of the Herd (1565)
teaser: Bruegel's cattle come down from the mountains as autumn darkens — the herd's slow descent mirrors the season's end. It is one of the surviving panels of his lost Months cycle.

exploreAction.targetName: The Return of the Herd (1565) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The cows and oxen file down the slope, their horns silhouetted against a gray October sky. The trees are bare, the people carry wood, the year is closing. Bruegel painted the seasons as a farmer knows them — as work, weather, and time running out.

name: The Gloomy Day (1565)
teaser: Bruegel's early-spring painting — the sky is heavy, the trees bare, a village floods, and people struggle with the year's first work. Winter is over; so is the relief of winter.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gloomy Day (1565) by Bruegel, Kunsthistorisches Museum
exploreAction.instruction: The storm is breaking over the flooded valley while villagers work in the foreground. Bruegel's 'gloomy day' is March — the month of mud and no excuses. The painting is a portrait of a season that refuses to be cheerful.

name: The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (c. 1833)
teaser: A series of 55 woodblock prints following the Tōkaidō road from Edo to Kyoto — the highway every traveler walked in feudal Japan. Hiroshige turned a practical journey into a poem of weather, inns, and pilgrims. Each print shows a different station, and the whole set became the best-selling ukiyo-e series in history. Van Gogh copied two of the prints in oil paint.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (c. 1833) by Utagawa Hiroshige
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō (c. 1833) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Cranes (c. 1750)
teaser: Two cranes in black ink on silk — one poised mid-step, the other preening — drawn with strokes so few and so sure they seem to have arrived fully formed. Sesshū trained as a Zen monk, and his paintings were acts of meditation; he is often called the greatest painter in Japanese history. The cranes' calm stillness is the point: emptiness made visible.

exploreAction.targetName: Cranes (c. 1750) by Sesshū Tōyō
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Cranes (c. 1750) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Tale of Genji Handscroll (c. 1130)
teaser: A painted scroll telling the story of the world's first novel — a Japanese court lady's tale of a prince and his many loves. The handscroll is read right to left, unrolled a section at a time so the viewer is inside the story. Faces are painted in a single line, deliberately expressionless, while the robes and architecture carry all the emotion. It survives in fragments, each one priceless.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tale of Genji Handscroll (c. 1130) by Unknown (Heian court painter)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Tale of Genji Handscroll (c. 1130) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Admonitions Scroll (c. 400-600)
teaser: The oldest surviving Chinese painting on silk — a handscroll of moral lessons for an empress, with figures drawn in flowing, calligraphic line. It survives in a copy from the Six Dynasties period, attributed to the legendary painter Gu Kaizhi. The scroll teaches virtue through story-pictures: a lady refusing a bear, a concubine cutting her hair to save her lord. It was nearly lost in a 1900 fire that destroyed much of the British Museum's Chinese collection.

exploreAction.targetName: Admonitions Scroll (c. 400-600) by Gu Kaizhi
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Admonitions Scroll (c. 400-600) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Tale of the Genji: Kashiwagi chapter (17th century)
teaser: A painted screen showing a stolen glance between a prince and his cousin's wife — the moment that starts a tragedy in the world's first novel. The artist compresses an entire emotional catastrophe into one glance across a garden. Screen painting allowed Japanese artists to combine text, calligraphy, and image in a single view. The scene's restraint is its power: nothing happens, and everything happens.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tale of the Genji: Kashiwagi chapter (17th century) by Tosa school
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Tale of the Genji: Kashiwagi chapter (17th century) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Persian Miniature: The Court of Gayumars (1522)
teaser: A page from the Shahnameh, the Persian book of kings, showing the first king of the world enthroned among courtiers and animals. The artist stacked time and space like a carpet — no perspective, every figure equal, all of nature in bloom. It is considered the finest page of the finest Persian manuscript ever made. Its colors — sky blues, cinnabar, gold — have survived five centuries because the pigments were ground from real stones.

exploreAction.targetName: Persian Miniature: The Court of Gayumars (1522) by Sultan Muhammad
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Persian Miniature: The Court of Gayumars (1522) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Bowl with Blue Splash Decoration (9th century)
teaser: A simple clay bowl glazed with three blue-green splashes — an accident of kiln chemistry that became a revolution. Tang dynasty potters in China discovered that a copper-oxide splash fired in the right kiln turned into jewel-blue. The style spread along the Silk Road to Persia, Egypt, and Spain, where it became known as 'splash ware.' A potter's mistake that outlived empires.

exploreAction.targetName: Bowl with Blue Splash Decoration (9th century) by Unknown (Tang dynasty)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Bowl with Blue Splash Decoration (9th century) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace (13th century)
teaser: A handscroll of fire and chaos — armed warriors storming a palace at night, flames rolling across the top of the picture while figures flee below. The painter compressed a real 1159 coup into one scrolling catastrophe, and the scroll reads like a movie storyboard. Horses gallop, bodies fall, the fire licks the border. It is one of the great action sequences in pre-modern art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace (13th century) by Unknown (Kamakura period)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace (13th century) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Uruk Vase (c. 3200 BCE)
teaser: The oldest known narrative artwork in the world — a carved alabaster vase from the first city, showing a procession of offerings to a goddess. The vase stacks reality like a ladder: water and grain at the bottom, sheep above, naked men carrying baskets, and the goddess receiving it all at the top. It is the first art we know of that tells a story in order. After the 2003 Iraq war, it was smashed into pieces and painstakingly restored.

exploreAction.targetName: The Uruk Vase (c. 3200 BCE) by Unknown (Sumerian)

name: The Royal Game of Ur (c. 2600 BCE)
teaser: A game board of shell and lapis inlaid in wood — the oldest complete board game ever found, with rules deciphered from a Babylonian clay tablet. Players raced pieces along a track of twenty squares, with some squares marked rosettes that granted extra moves. It was played for 3,000 years, from Sumer to Babylon. A museum curator translated the rules in 1982, and the game is playable again today.

exploreAction.targetName: The Royal Game of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) by Unknown (Sumerian)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Royal Game of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE)
teaser: A granite slab carved with the earliest mention of Israel in any surviving text — a pharaoh boasting that 'Israel is laid waste, its seed is not.' Found in Thebes, it is the only reference to ancient Israel in Egyptian records. The stele's boast is questionable — the same text was recycled from an earlier monument, a common Egyptian shortcut. It remains a cornerstone of biblical archaeology.

exploreAction.targetName: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) by Unknown (Egyptian)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BCE) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE)
teaser: A slab of black granodiorite carrying the same decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, demotic, and Greek. Its discovery gave scholars the key to reading Egyptian writing after 1,500 years of silence. Thomas Young cracked the phonetic value of some signs; Jean-François Champollion finished the job in 1822. The stone has been on display in the British Museum since 1802 and is the museum's most visited object.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) by Unknown (Ptolemaic)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Nabonidus Cylinder (c. 550 BCE)
teaser: A clay cylinder on which Babylon's last king recorded his restoration of temples and his dream of seeing them stand forever. The text lists repairs to the sanctuary of the moon god and prays for the king's own name to endure. The cylinder was buried in a foundation, meant to be read by future kings — a time capsule. Babylon fell to Cyrus shortly after; the cylinder outlasted the kingdom.

exploreAction.targetName: The Nabonidus Cylinder (c. 550 BCE) by Unknown (Babylonian)
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Nabonidus Cylinder (c. 550 BCE) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Oxus Treasure: Golden Griffin Armlet (5th century BCE)
teaser: A pair of gold armlets ending in winged griffins, found buried in a hoard beside the Oxus river in Central Asia. Each griffin is hammered from sheet gold, with gem-set eyes and inlaid wings. The hoard is the most important surviving collection of Achaemenid Persian gold. The armlets were probably ceremonial rather than practical — too fragile to wear in battle, too precious to wear casually.

Vollard, who handled Cézanne and Gauguin, sat for Picasso 22 times while his face was systematically broken apart and rebuilt. Picasso said the portrait shows the dealer 'from every side at once.' It marks the peak of analytic Cubism, six years before the movement dissolved. Even the subject, a great connoisseur, could not tell if he liked it.

name: Man with a Guitar (1912)
teaser: A guitar and a man flattened into a fan of brown planes, with the guitar's sound hole painted as a real hole in the canvas — Picasso's most elegant Cubist still life. He pasted actual paper and cloth into the painting, inventing collage in the process. The painting is an object about objects: painted wood grain pretending to be real wood, a hole pretending to be a hole. The critic said the painting 'smells of turpentine and sawdust.' It is a guitar you can hear.

name: Still Life with Chair Caning (1912)

He signed it with a piece of newspaper lettering. Every collage, every mixed-media artwork since, descends from this small oval painting.

name: The City Rises (1910)

The white is not empty; it is the space where the shapes breathe. Kandinsky wrote that the painting explores 'the opposition of the sharp and the soft.' He was teaching at the Bauhaus and thinking about how a picture could be as precise as music. The red circle is the note that makes the whole composition sing.

name: The Ghent Altarpiece: Adoration of the Mystic Lamb (1432)
teaser: The most stolen artwork in history — a twelve-panel altarpiece with a central panel where crowds of martyrs, popes, and pilgrims stream toward a lamb on an altar. The brothers van Eyck completed it in 1432, and its oil technique changed painting forever. The altarpiece has been looted, hidden, sold, and dismantled a dozen times; the Nazis stole it, and the 'Monuments Men' recovered it. One panel, The Just Judges, was stolen in 1934 and never found. The altarpiece is still in Ghent, where it has been for six centuries.

The painting is full of gold-leaf details that still gleam. It established Botticelli as Florence's finest painter.

name: Madonna of the Meadow (1506)
teaser: Mary seated on the ground between the infant Jesus and the infant John, her face serene, her feet bare — Raphael's painting of divine motherhood as ordinary tenderness. The landscape behind is soft Umbrian hills, and the composition is a perfect triangle. Raphael was 23, and the painting shows him absorbing Leonardo's lessons: the softer modeling, the deeper space. The two babies' closeness and the cross in John's hand hint at the future. It is one of the most loved Madonnas ever painted.

exploreAction.targetName: Madonna of the Meadow (1506) by Raphael
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Madonna of the Meadow (1506) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Entombment (1507)
teaser: Christ's body carried to the tomb by four straining men, with a Mary whose grief is almost theatrical — Raphael's early masterpiece, painted when he was 24. The composition was copied by every painter in Rome, and it made his reputation. The figures' poses are borrowed from classical sculpture, giving the grief a heroic structure. The painting's emotional force is so great that it was later claimed by Napoleon's troops and sent to Paris. It returned to Rome in 1815.

exploreAction.targetName: The Entombment (1507) by Raphael
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Entombment (1507) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Barque of Dante (1822)
teaser: Dante and Virgil crossing the river of hell in a small boat, with the damned clutching the gunwale — Delacroix's first great painting, made when he was 24. The painting was a homage to Géricault and Michelangelo, and it made Delacroix famous overnight. The corpses' faces in the water are borrowed from Michelangelo's Last Judgment. The Louvre bought it immediately, an unusual honor for a young painter. It remains the definitive image of entering hell.

exploreAction.targetName: The Barque of Dante (1822) by Eugène Delacroix
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Barque of Dante (1822) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Valpinçon Bather (1808)
teaser: A woman seen from behind, seated on the edge of a bed, her back a single flawless curve — Ingres's study of the nude as pure form. The painting has no story, no background, no face: just a back, a turban, and a bath. Critics and artists have called it the most beautiful back in Western art. Ingres painted it in Rome and kept it in his studio for years. Degas and Picasso both copied it; its calm perfection made it a touchstone of classical drawing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Valpinçon Bather (1808) by Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Valpinçon Bather (1808) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Oedipus and the Sphinx (1864)
teaser: The hero facing the monster — a winged sphinx with a woman's head and a lion's body, perched above him in a narrow pass. Moreau's painting turns the Greek myth into a psychological duel: the sphinx's claws on Oedipus's chest, his hand raised in refusal. The painting is the centerpiece of Symbolism, the movement that painted ideas rather than scenes. Moreau painted the sphinx's face as beautiful and fatal. It is the image of every question that cannot be answered.

exploreAction.targetName: Oedipus and the Sphinx (1864) by Gustave Moreau
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Oedipus and the Sphinx (1864) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Isle of the Dead (1880)
teaser: A dark island of cypresses rising from a still sea, with a white figure rowing a coffin toward a shore of rock — Böcklin's most famous painting, painted in five versions. The image of death as a quiet island struck Europe so hard that reproductions hung in a million homes; Hitler later kept one in the Reich Chancellery. The painting is pure mood: no drama, no figure beyond the rower, just the silence of arrival. Rachmaninoff composed a symphonic poem inspired by it. It is the most haunted landscape ever painted.

exploreAction.targetName: The Isle of the Dead (1880) by Arnold Böcklin
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Isle of the Dead (1880) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Course of Empire: The Consummation (1836)
teaser: A gleaming marble city at the height of its power, with a triumphant procession crossing the bay — the middle panel of Thomas Cole's five-painting series about the rise and fall of a civilization. The series shows the same landscape from savage wilderness to pastoral settlement to imperial glory to destruction to ruin. Cole invented the idea that a landscape could tell a story over time. The paintings hang in the New-York Historical Society as a complete set, one of the great series in American art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Course of Empire: The Consummation (1836) by Thomas Cole
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Course of Empire: The Consummation (1836) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Almond Blossom (1890)
teaser: White blossoms on bare branches against a pure blue sky — van Gogh's painting for his newborn nephew, the only painting he ever made in pure joy. He painted it in the asylum's garden, where an almond tree was blooming early. The composition is borrowed from Japanese prints he loved: the branches cropped by the frame, the flat blue background. He wrote to his brother that the painting was for the baby, 'so that he can start on the same branch as the others.' Van Gogh died months later; the blossoms survived.

exploreAction.targetName: Almond Blossom (1890) by Vincent van Gogh
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Almond Blossom (1890) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Vision after the Sermon (1888)
teaser: Breton women in white bonnets leaving a church and seeing, in a vision, Jacob wrestling an angel — Gauguin's painting of faith made visible. The women are in the foreground, the wrestling match in a red field behind them, separated from reality by a tree trunk. The red field is the field of the vision, not of Brittany. Gauguin wrote that he wanted 'the naïveté of the primitive' and got it: the painting looks like a folk print elevated to philosophy. It is the founding work of his Synthetist style.

exploreAction.targetName: Vision after the Sermon (1888) by Paul Gauguin
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Vision after the Sermon (1888) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Mont Sainte-Victoire seen from Les Lauves (1906)
teaser: The mountain Cézanne painted over eighty times, reduced in this last version to a veil of shifting planes of color — the painting that ended the 19th century and began the 20th. From his studio above Aix, he painted the mountain until it dissolved into pure structure. The painting's strokes are parallel, almost systematic, like a code. Cézanne said he wanted to 'treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere, the cone.' The mountain he painted here is barely a mountain anymore; it is painting itself.

exploreAction.targetName: Mont Sainte-Victoire seen from Les Lauves (1906) by Paul Cézanne
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Mont Sainte-Victoire seen from Les Lauves (1906) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: Still Life with Apples and Oranges (1899)
teaser: A tablecloth, a basket, and a pyramid of fruit that tilts toward the viewer from every direction at once — Cézanne's still life that broke perspective forever. The apples are painted from different angles, the tabletop is tilted, the cloth is a glacier of folds. Cézanne worked on his still lifes for months, arranging and rearranging the fruit until it was 'just right.' He said he wanted to 'astonish Paris with an apple.' The painting's instability is its genius: the world seen truly, which is never stable.

exploreAction.targetName: Still Life with Apples and Oranges (1899) by Paul Cézanne
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across Still Life with Apples and Oranges (1899) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte (1884)
teaser: Hundreds of Parisians enjoying a Sunday in the park, painted in tiny dots of pure color that blend in the eye — Seurat's masterpiece, the most famous pointillist painting ever made. He spent two years painting it, and the canvas is over six feet wide. The figures are stiff as statues, the light is frozen, and the whole scene has the stillness of a museum diorama. Seurat called the technique 'chromo-luminarism'; the public called it 'confetti.' The painting made him famous at 27 and has been a cultural icon ever since.

exploreAction.targetName: A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte (1884) by Georges Seurat
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte (1884) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Circus (1891)
teaser: A ringmaster, a rider on a galloping horse, a clown, and an audience reduced to dots — Seurat's last painting, left unfinished when he died of meningitis at 31. The composition is pure geometry: the circus ring is a wheel, the performers are arcs and spirals. Seurat painted it in the last months of his life, in the pointillist style pushed to the edge of abstraction. The painting's frozen motion is the point: the circus caught mid-leap, forever. It hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, unfinished, with the white gaps showing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Circus (1891) by Georges Seurat
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Circus (1891) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Medical Inspection (1894)
teaser: A line of prostitutes waiting for a doctor's exam in a brothel, painted by Toulouse-Lautrec who lived in brothels for years — a painting of women being processed like cattle. He was the only major artist to paint the profession's routine, its boredom and humiliation. The women's faces are blank, their bodies tired, the doctor unseen. Lautrec's perspective flattens the room into a diagram. The painting was too raw for public display for decades. It is social documentary as high art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Medical Inspection (1894) by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Medical Inspection (1894) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Boating Party (1893)
teaser: A mother and child in a boat, the mother rowing, the child's legs kicking, the river and the parasol blazing — Cassatt's painting of motherhood as active life, not still life. Cassatt was the only American in the Impressionist circle, and she painted women as agents: reading, rowing, caring, working. The painting's high viewpoint and cropping are borrowed from Japanese prints. The mother's face is the model's; the child is her nephew. It is the most famous American Impressionist painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Boating Party (1893) by Mary Cassatt
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Boating Party (1893) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Child's Bath (1893)
teaser: A mother bathing a child in a basin, their heads close together, the composition seen from above like a Japanese print — Cassatt's most famous painting of the bond between mother and child. The pattern of the wallpaper, the gown, and the rug flatten the scene into a decorative whole. Cassatt used the high viewpoint to make the two figures a single shape of tenderness. The painting was exhibited at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and is now in the Art Institute of Chicago. It is the definitive image of maternal care in American art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Child's Bath (1893) by Mary Cassatt
exploreAction.instruction: Let your eyes wander across The Child's Bath (1893) in silence for a moment, then notice one detail you have never seen before — a brushstroke, a shadow, a figure in the corner. Ask what the artist wanted you to feel standing here, and let the work answer.

name: The Milkmaid (1658)
teaser: A kitchen maid pouring milk with a concentration so still that the room seems to hold its breath. Vermeer painted the light itself — the window's cool daylight, the bread's crust, the nail shadow on the wall. The maid is not looking at anything, and that is the whole subject.

exploreAction.targetName: The Milkmaid (1658) up close
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the wall behind the maid — the light there is Vermeer's real subject, not the figure. Notice how the nail's shadow tells you exactly where the window is.

name: The Laughing Cavalier (1624)
teaser: A portrait so lively that the sitter seems about to speak — the swaggering pose, the tilted hat, the embroidered sleeve painted with astonishing speed. The title is a mistake: the man is not laughing, just smirking. Hals's loose brushwork made him the anti-thesis of stiff court portraiture.

exploreAction.targetName: The Laughing Cavalier (1624) details
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sleeve's embroidery — Hals painted it with quick, confident strokes that read as detail only from a distance. Notice how the pose breaks the portrait's 'still life' rule.

name: Primavera (1482)
teaser: Nine mythological figures in an orange grove: Venus at the centre, the Three Graces dancing, Mercury dispersing clouds, and Flora scattering flowers from her dress. Nobody agrees what it means — a wedding allegory, a Neoplatonic poem, a calendar of spring. It was rediscovered in a country villa after 400 years of obscurity.

exploreAction.targetName: Primavera (1482) figure by figure
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Three Graces — the painting's movement all lives in their dance. Then notice Zephyr, the wind god on the right: the painting starts and ends with him.

name: The Vitruvian Man (1490)
teaser: The perfect human: a man inscribed in both a circle and a square, Leonardo's attempt to prove that the human body follows geometry. Based on the Roman architect Vitruvius's proportions, it is part anatomy study, part manifesto. The drawing survives in Venice, and the image has become the symbol of humanism itself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Vitruvian Man (1490) proportions
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two poses — arms outstretched in a square, then raised in a circle — and notice the notes: Leonardo wrote the proportions beside the figure in mirror script.

name: The Woman in Gold (1907)
teaser: Adele Bloch-Bauer's portrait, a shimmering mosaic of gold leaf, spirals and Egyptian motifs — the most expensive painting ever sold when it fetched $135 million in 2006. It was looted by the Nazis, and the fight to recover it became a landmark restitution case. Klimt painted Adele twice; this is the first, more famous, version.

exploreAction.targetName: The Woman in Gold (1907) gold details
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the gold is not just background but texture — every patch of leaf catches light differently. Notice Adele's hands, folded so tightly they disappear into the pattern.

name: Oath of the Horatii (1784)
teaser: Three Roman brothers swear on their father's swords to defend Rome — while the women weep behind them. David's neo-classical masterpiece made him the most famous painter in Europe and a revolutionary propaganda machine. The rigid geometry of the composition was deliberate: it is about duty crushing feeling.

exploreAction.targetName: Oath of the Horatii (1784) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two halves of the canvas: the rigid, vertical men versus the slumped, curved women. The painting is a diagram of a moral argument, not a scene.

name: The Monk by the Sea (1810)
teaser: A lone monk facing an almost empty horizon — sky, sea, sand, and one tiny figure. The painting reduces landscape to its absolute minimum, which is exactly why it terrified viewers at the time. Heinrich von Kleist called it 'the sublime in a state of stillness'. The monk's back is turned: we are meant to take his place.

exploreAction.targetName: The Monk by the Sea (1810) emptiness
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how little is actually painted — the composition is almost empty, and the figure is a vertical dash. That emptiness is the subject; stand in the monk's place.

name: The Kiss (1898)
teaser: Two lovers frozen mid-embrace, carved from white marble so smooth it looks wet. Rodin based it on Dante's Paolo and Francesca — lovers who were killed for their affair. The original stands in the Rodin Museum; the embrace is so complete that faces almost disappear into the stone.

exploreAction.targetName: The Kiss (1898) marble carving
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the figures melt into each other — the marble is carved so the boundary between them blurs. Then walk around it: the composition changes from every angle.

name: Balloon Dog (2013)
teaser: A 10-foot steel sculpture of a balloon animal, polished to a mirror shine — one of five coloured editions, each a different colour. The orange version sold for $58.4 million, then the most expensive sculpture by a living artist. It looks like a child's party trick blown up to monumental scale, which is exactly the point.

exploreAction.targetName: Balloon Dog (2013) mirrored surface
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the reflections — the polished steel makes the sculpture a funhouse mirror of the room. Then walk around it: it reads as weightless metal, which it is not.

name: Brillo Box (1964)
teaser: Wooden boxes stacked like supermarket stock, screen-printed with the Brillo pad logo — indistinguishable from the real thing until you touch them. Warhol's point was that the factory and the gallery now made the same object. The philosopher Arthur Danto used it to ask what makes art art: 'the Brillo box' became philosophy's favourite example.

exploreAction.targetName: Brillo Box (1964) up close
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the difference between this and the real product — there is almost none, which is the point. Then consider: what did Warhol add by hand-making a factory object?

name: No. 5, 1948
teaser: A 2.4-metre web of dripped paint — beige, grey and red lines tangled so densely the surface looks like a map of weather. Pollock laid the canvas on the floor and poured from above, making the first 'action painting'. It sold for $140 million in 2006, then the most expensive painting ever.

exploreAction.targetName: No. 5, 1948 (1948) drip structure
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the depth — layers of drips overlap into a dense weave, not a flat pattern. Notice how the red cuts through the grey like a lightning strike.

name: Number 1A (1948)
teaser: Pollock's breakthrough: the first painting where he abandoned the easel entirely and poured paint across a floor canvas — the moment abstract expressionism was born. Black and white enamel tangled with skeins of colour, the whole surface in motion. It entered MoMA in 1951 as the museum's first major Pollock purchase.

exploreAction.targetName: Number 1A (1948) poured-paint surface
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the black enamel lines — they run on top of the colour like drawn ink. Then step back: the chaos resolves into a rhythm of loops and drips.

name: Bal du moulin de la Galette (1876)
teaser: A Sunday dance at a Montmartre windmill — friends, workers and dancers under dappled light, painted with the loose brushwork that made Renoir the Impressionists' most joyful member. The light filtering through the trees is the real subject: it falls on shoulders, hats and faces in scattered dots.

exploreAction.targetName: Bal du moulin de la Galette (1876) light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light patches — Renoir painted the shade of the trees as blobs of colour on clothes and faces. Then find the girl in blue at the front: she was a real laundress he knew.

name: Luncheon on the Grass (1863)
teaser: A nude woman picnicking with two fully dressed men — the painting that scandalized Paris and helped launch modern art. The figures are real people in a real setting, deliberately mismatched, with classical poses quoted from Raphael. The Salon rejected it; the public laughed at it; art never looked the same.

exploreAction.targetName: Luncheon on the Grass (1863) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the tonal logic: the woman's skin matches the man's shirt, and the fruit in the foreground echoes the nude. The outrage was the point — Manet wanted to provoke.

name: The Third-Class Carriage (1864)
teaser: Working Parisians packed into a railway carriage — a grandmother, a nursing mother, exhausted labourers — painted with the empathy that made Daumier the century's great social observer. The light falls on the family's faces, not the crowd. It is one of the earliest paintings of the everyday poor as a serious subject.

exploreAction.targetName: The Third-Class Carriage (1864) faces
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the three generations in the foreground — the grandmother's face is carved by labour. Then notice how the crowd behind dissolves into shadow, keeping the family the focus.

name: Erased de Kooning Drawing (1953)
teaser: A drawing by Willem de Kooning that Rauschenberg erased — carefully, over a month, leaving only smudges in a gold frame. De Kooning gave him the drawing knowing it would be destroyed. It is one of the most radical gestures in art: the first conceptual artwork, where the act matters more than the object.

exploreAction.targetName: Erased de Kooning Drawing (1953) traces
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the residue — faint graphite lines that were once a drawing. The frame is the museum case for a crime scene: the artwork is the absence itself.

name: Dove (1949)
teaser: A hanging mobile of cut steel and wire that drifts in the air currents — part sculpture, part weather vane. Calder invented the mobile in the 1930s, giving sculpture the one thing it never had: motion. This one hangs in the Museum of Modern Art, and its balance is so fine that a breath sets it moving.

exploreAction.targetName: Dove (1949) mobile balance
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the painted shapes balance each other — each arm of the mobile is tuned like a scale. Then wait: the piece never hangs still twice.

name: Untitled (I Shop Therefore I Am) (1987)
teaser: White-on-red text over a storefront hand — a slogan that reads like a corporate ad and hits like a diagnosis. Kruger's work pastes feminist critique into the visual language of advertising: big type, borrowed photographs, punchlines that bite. 'I shop therefore I am' remains her most quoted line.

exploreAction.targetName: Untitled (I Shop Therefore I Am) (1987) text
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the piece borrows advertising's exact look — red background, white type — so the critique lands inside the language it attacks.

name: Bicycle Wheel (1913)
teaser: A bicycle wheel mounted on a kitchen stool — the first 'readymade': a factory object declared art by an artist's choice. Duchamp made it not to be beautiful but to ask what art is. Spinning the wheel was the point: the movement was the sculpture. It changed art's question from 'how?' to 'why?'.

exploreAction.targetName: Bicycle Wheel (1913) readymade
exploreAction.instruction: Look at it as Duchamp did: the wheel and stool are nothing special — the art is the choice to put them together. Then spin the wheel; the motion is half the piece.

name: Lobster Telephone (1936)
teaser: A working telephone with a plaster lobster glued to the receiver — Dalí's surrealist joke about sexual frustration and communication. He chose the lobster because it looked like a phone's handset and was 'in love' with telephones. One version sits in the Tate; it famously still rings, when the museum lets it.

exploreAction.targetName: Lobster Telephone (1936) absurdity
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the unlikely pairing — a crustacean and a telephone — and let the question sit: why does it feel like it should work? That unease is surrealism's engine.

name: Mae West Lips Sofa (1937)
teaser: A sofa shaped like the lips of actress Mae West, pink and pouting, designed by Dalí for his own living room. It was part of a whole room built around West's face. The lips are exactly the right size to sit on — the absurdity is that they're furniture. A surrealist's tribute to the most famous mouth in Hollywood.

exploreAction.targetName: Mae West Lips Sofa (1937) form
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the scale — the lips are life-size, so sitting on them feels transgressive. Notice how the furniture's function makes the surrealism stick.

name: Angel of the North (1998)
teaser: A 20-metre steel angel with wings angled like a plane's, standing over a Gateshead motorway — 200 tonnes of weathering steel with the footprint of a jumbo jet. Gormley based the pose on his own body. It is one of the most visited public sculptures in Britain, and its rusted colour is intentional: the steel is designed to oxidize.

exploreAction.targetName: Angel of the North (1998) in situ
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the wings' angle — tilted forward, not spread flat, so the angel reads as about to take off. Then notice the rust: it is the steel's protective coat, meant to be.

name: The Kelpies (2013)
teaser: Two 30-metre horse-head sculptures rising beside a canal in Falkirk — the largest equine sculptures in the world, each made of 600 tonnes of steel plates. They depict kelpies, shape-shifting water spirits from Scottish folklore. The heads are built from over 900 individual plates, each one curved like a living animal's hide.

exploreAction.targetName: The Kelpies (2013) steel plates
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the plates are angled to catch light differently — the heads shimmer as you walk around them. Then notice the scale: the horse's eye is taller than a person.

name: Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss (1793)
teaser: Cupid leaning over the sleeping Psyche, lifting her hair to wake her with a kiss — marble carved so finely that the cloth looks soft and the skin looks warm. Canova's neo-classical masterpiece is built like a spiral: walk around it and the embrace unfolds in a continuous line. It was commissioned by a British colonel who never took delivery.

exploreAction.targetName: Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss (1793) spiral
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sculpture's spiral composition — from every angle the two bodies form a different continuous line. Then look at Psyche's hand: it reaches up to touch Cupid's face mid-dream.

name: The Rape of Proserpina (1622)
teaser: Pluto's hand gripping Proserpina's thigh so convincingly that the marble seems to dent — Bernini was 23 when he carved it. The abduction of Proserpina into the underworld explains winter in Greek myth. The sculpture's drama is the point: every muscle strained, every finger pressing into real flesh.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rape of Proserpina (1622) marble illusion
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fingers pressing into Proserpina's thigh — the marble is carved so the flesh appears to give way. That illusion of softness in hard stone is Bernini's whole game.

name: Apollo and Daphne (1625)
teaser: The moment Daphne transforms into a laurel tree to escape Apollo — her fingers sprouting leaves, her legs turning to bark, her mouth opening mid-metamorphosis. Bernini carved the transition so finely that the stone seems to be changing as you watch. The sculpture is designed to be circled: the story unfolds as you walk.

exploreAction.targetName: Apollo and Daphne (1625) transformation
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the hands and feet — leaves growing from fingers, roots from toes. Then walk around the base: the chase and the transformation read as a sequence, not a still.

name: The Lion of Lucerne (1821)
teaser: A dying lion carved into a cliff face in Lucerne, a spear in its flank, mourning the Swiss Guards who fell defending the Tuileries in 1792. Mark Twain called it 'the most mournful and moving piece of stone in the world'. The 10-metre relief was carved directly into the sandstone of the quarry where the stone was cut.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lion of Lucerne (1821) relief
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lion's face — grief rendered at monumental scale. Then notice the shield bearing the fleur-de-lis: the sculpture mourns a loyalty that ended in massacre.

name: Mount Rushmore (1941)
teaser: Four presidents carved into a South Dakota mountain — Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt and Lincoln — each face 18 metres tall, visible for miles. Borglum blew off 450,000 tons of rock with dynamite, then refined the faces with jackhammers. It took 14 years and the original plan called for the presidents down to their waists.

exploreAction.targetName: Mount Rushmore (1941) carving technique
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the scale: each face is the height of a six-storey building, and the eyes are large enough to hold a person. The granite was chosen because it weathers slowly.

name: Christ the Redeemer (1931)
teaser: The 30-metre Art Deco Christ on Corcovado mountain, watching over Rio de Janeiro — built from reinforced concrete and six million soapstone tiles, engineered by the French sculptor Landowski and the Brazilian Heitor da Silva Costa. The statue is struck by lightning several times a year and has been repaired repeatedly. It is one of the New Seven Wonders.

exploreAction.targetName: Christ the Redeemer (1931) engineering
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the outstretched arms — the span is 28 metres, wider than the statue is tall. Then notice the soapstone mosaic: thousands of tiles, each cut by hand to follow the body.

name: The Motherland Calls (1967)
teaser: An 85-metre sword-wielding woman on the Volga — the tallest statue in the world when built, and still the tallest of a woman. She marks the site of the Battle of Stalingrad, the deadliest battle in history. The sword alone is 33 metres and weighs 14 tons. Engineers had to brace the figure's base after the foundations settled.

exploreAction.targetName: The Motherland Calls (1967) scale
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the figure's forward stride — she is stepping toward the Volga, calling the soldiers forward. Then look up: the raised sword makes the statue visible from kilometres away.

name: The Falling Soldier (1936)
teaser: A Republican militiaman at the instant a bullet hits him — the most famous war photograph ever taken, and one of the most debated. Capa shot it on a Spanish hillside in 1936; sceptics later argued it was staged. Whoever is right, the image fixed the Spanish Civil War in the world's memory. The identity of the soldier was only established decades later.

exploreAction.targetName: The Falling Soldier (1936) context
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the falling body's geometry — the rifle, the arm, the ground all meeting at one point. Then read the debate: the photo's power survives even the doubt about its staging.

name: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima (1945)
teaser: Six Marines raising the Stars and Stripes on Mount Suribachi — the most reproduced photograph in American history, model for the Marine Corps War Memorial. Rosenthal shot it almost by instinct, then worried he'd missed it. Three of the six men died days later on the island. It won the Pulitzer and became a symbol of the Pacific war.

exploreAction.targetName: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima (1945) story
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the composition — the pole's diagonal against the sky, the six men braced as one. Then read the caption drama: the photo was nearly never taken, and nearly misidentified after.

name: V-J Day in Times Square (1945)
teaser: A sailor kissing a nurse in Times Square on the day the war ended — the war's most joyful photograph, snapped by Eisenstaedt in seconds while scanning for a shot. Neither subject was ever reliably identified for decades; several sailors and nurses claimed the roles. The kiss was a stranger's impulse, frozen as a nation's release.

exploreAction.targetName: V-J Day in Times Square (1945) story
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the spontaneity — the sailor's bent back, the nurse's lifted leg, everyone around them celebrating. Then consider the debate: who exactly they were stayed a mystery for fifty years.

name: Dali Atomicus (1948)
teaser: Salvador Dalí frozen mid-air beside a floating chair, three cats and a bucket of water — an image that took six hours and 28 attempts, with assistants throwing cats and water on cue. The photograph was a response to the atomic age: everything hovering, nothing touching. The final print shows the thrown water and the cats' terror mid-flight.

exploreAction.targetName: Dali Atomicus (1948) outtakes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at what is airborne — Dalí, the chair, the easel, the cats, the water — everything defying gravity. Then know: it took 28 takes and the studio was soaked by the time it worked.

name: The Burning Monk (1963)
teaser: Thích Quảng Đức, a Buddhist monk, immolating himself in a Saigon intersection to protest the South Vietnamese government's persecution of Buddhists. Associated Press photographer Malcolm Browne's image circled the world within hours. President Kennedy later said the photo influenced US policy more than any report. It won the Pulitzer and is among the century's most consequential images.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burning Monk (1963) story
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the stillness of the figure amid the flames — the monk does not move as the fire takes him. Then read what came after: the image changed the course of a war.

name: Earthrise (1968)
teaser: The Earth rising over the Moon's horizon, photographed from Apollo 8 — the first time humans saw their whole planet from another world. The crew were orbiting the Moon when the sight appeared; Anders grabbed a camera with colour film on impulse. The image helped birth the environmental movement: a fragile blue marble in black space.

exploreAction.targetName: Earthrise (1968) story
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the contrast — the grey lunar horizon against the blue-white Earth. Then sit with the effect: no one had seen this before, and it changed how we see home.

name: The Blue Marble (1972)
teaser: The full Earth, cloud-swirled and sunlit, photographed from 45,000 kilometres away by the Apollo 17 crew — the last time humans travelled far enough to see the whole planet in one frame. It became the most reproduced photograph in history, the icon of the environmental era. It was taken, almost casually, on the mission's way out.

exploreAction.targetName: The Blue Marble (1972) story
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the weather systems — the swirls are real storms wrapping the planet. Then notice: no human has seen this exact view since 1972.

name: Water Lilies (1916)
teaser: One panel from Monet's obsessive final project: the lily pond at Giverny, painted hundreds of times as his eyesight failed. The surface dissolves into pure colour — reflections of sky, willow and cloud mixed with the pads. Monet gave a set of the giant panels to France as a peace offering after the First World War; they hang in the Orangerie in a curved room.

exploreAction.targetName: Water Lilies (1916) surface
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the painting's surface as water — there is no horizon, no sky, just reflection. Monet painted the same pond for thirty years as it became less a place and more an idea.

name: The Supper at Emmaus (1601)
teaser: The moment two disciples recognize the risen Christ — and the table explodes: the basket tips, the man lunges, and light blasts from Christ's bare head. Caravaggio painted the scene as a street-level miracle in a dark inn, not a heavenly vision. The realism — dusty clothes, cracked bread, an innkeeper who has no idea what's happening — is the point.

exploreAction.targetName: The Supper at Emmaus (1601) light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light source: it comes from Christ himself, not the window. Then notice the still-life — the fruit basket teeters at the table's edge, a moment away from spilling.

name: The Cardsharps (1594)
teaser: A naive boy losing a card game to a cheat who signals his partner from behind — painted when Caravaggio was in his early twenties and broke. The picture is a manual of deception: the cheat hides a card behind his back while the older man peers at the boy's hand. It made Caravaggio's name and invented the genre of low-life scenes.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cardsharps (1594) details
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the three faces — each tells a different story of the same game. Then find the hidden card and the finger signals: the painting is a crime diagram.

name: The Return of the Prodigal Son (1668)
teaser: The father's hands on his returned son's shoulders — one hand strong, one hand soft, a lifetime of forgiveness in a single gesture. Rembrandt painted it near the end of his life, broke and bereaved, and it shows: the light falls only on the embrace. The elder brother stands apart in shadow, excluded by his own resentment.

exploreAction.targetName: The Return of the Prodigal Son (1668) hands
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the father's two hands — different pressures, different meanings. Then notice the composition: every figure is still, and the whole painting rests on one gesture.

name: The Jewish Bride (1665)
teaser: A couple so absorbed in each other that the viewer is a trespasser — his hand flat on her breast, her hand covering his. The title is a guess; the subjects are unknown. Rembrandt painted the cloth with such thick strokes that the robe's gold seems to glow from within. Van Gogh said he'd give ten years of his life to sit and stare at it.

exploreAction.targetName: The Jewish Bride (1665) texture
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the gold sleeve — Rembrandt's paint is so thick it catches real light, not just painted light. Then notice the tenderness: the couple's eyes are averted, lost in each other.

name: Self-Portrait with Two Circles (1665)
teaser: The last and greatest of Rembrandt's self-portraits: the ageing painter, brush and palette in hand, standing before two chalk circles on a wall. Nobody agrees what the circles mean — the world, the eye, the perfect line no artist can draw. The face is unsparing: he painted himself as he was, not as he wished to be seen.

exploreAction.targetName: Self-Portrait with Two Circles (1665) the circles
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the circles — blank, perfect, unexplained. Then look at the face: sixty years of self-scrutiny, rendered without flattery. The painting is a question no one has answered.

name: The Mill (1645)
teaser: A windmill on a rise against a storm-lit sky — one of Rembrandt's few pure landscapes, and the only one that reads as a monument. The mill is dark against the light, its arms catching the last of the sun. For two centuries it was considered Rembrandt's greatest landscape and the equal of any history painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mill (1645) sky
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky — the storm and the light are fighting over the mill. Then notice how the windmill's dark silhouette makes it a character, not a backdrop.

name: The Polish Rider (1655)
teaser: A young rider in a fur cap and Eastern dress riding through a dark landscape — no one knows who he is, where he's going, or whether Rembrandt even painted the horse. The uncertainty has never dimmed its power: the rider is youth itself, lit against the gloom. It is the most enigmatic of Rembrandt's works.

exploreAction.targetName: The Polish Rider (1655) mystery
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the rider's face — serene, unreadable, lit from an unknown source. Then weigh the attribution debate: even the horse's authorship is argued, and the mystery is part of the art.

name: The Little Dancer of Fourteen Years (1881)
teaser: A bronze ballerina in a real tutu, real slippers and a real ribbon — the only sculpture Degas exhibited in his lifetime, and it scandalized Paris. Critics called her ugly, a monkey, a rat of the opera. Degas modelled her in wax with actual fabric; the bronzes were cast only after his death. She stands with her chin up, and she has never stopped being judged.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Dancer of Fourteen Years (1881) materials
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the real fabric — the tutu is not carved, it's sewn. Then meet her gaze: Degas gave a working child of the ballet a dignity the critics refused her.

name: Ballet Rehearsal (1873)
teaser: Dancers at the Paris Opera rehearsing in a wash of diffused light — some practising, some waiting, some adjusting a shoe. Degas painted the ballet hundreds of times, always as labour rather than spectacle: the discipline, the boredom, the ache. The composition is deliberately off-centre, a snapshot before snapshots existed.

exploreAction.targetName: Ballet Rehearsal (1873) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the empty space in the centre — the action happens around the gap, not in it. Then notice the waiting dancers: the ballet's unglamorous half is Degas's real subject.

name: The Railway (1873)
teaser: A woman with a book and a sleeping puppy at the new Gare Saint-Lazare, a girl watching steam through the fence — the modern city as a subject for art. Manet's friend Victorine Meurent posed for the woman; the steam is painted as white clouds, not smoke. The painting is about looking at what's behind a fence and never seeing it.

exploreAction.targetName: The Railway (1873) steam
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the steam — it fills the background like weather, hiding the trains entirely. Then notice the girl at the fence: she sees what we can't, and the painting never tells us what it is.

name: Music in the Tuileries (1862)
teaser: A crowd at a Paris park concert — not a single famous face, but a society caught in paint: artists, critics, composers and dandies mingling under the trees. Manet painted himself and his friends into the crowd, and the picture is one of the first modern paintings of modern leisure. The music is nowhere to be seen; the occasion is everything.

exploreAction.targetName: Music in the Tuileries (1862) crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the crowd as a cast list — Manet's friends are all here, including the painter himself. Then notice the format: a frieze of society, with the trees doing the composition.

name: The Execution of Emperor Maximilian (1867)
teaser: A firing squad executing the French-installed emperor of Mexico — a contemporary political atrocity painted as a flat, dispassionate line of men and rifles. Manet based it on newspaper accounts and a photograph of the execution. The Mexican soldiers wear French uniforms, a bitter joke about who really pulled the trigger. The French state suppressed it for years.

exploreAction.targetName: The Execution of Emperor Maximilian (1867) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the execution squad — they wear French uniforms, Manet's accusation aimed at his own government. Then notice the flatness: the horror is delivered without drama.

name: The Rue Mosnier with Flags (1878)
teaser: A Paris street hung with tricolour flags on a national holiday — and, in the foreground, a one-legged man on crutches crossing through the celebration. The flags are the joy; the crippled man is the cost. Manet painted the same street several times; only this version includes the passer-by who makes it a statement.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rue Mosnier with Flags (1878) the man
exploreAction.instruction: Look for the man on crutches in the foreground — the painting's title promises celebration, and he punctures it. Then notice the flags: painted in a single confident pass, each one a stroke of colour.

name: The Houses of Parliament series (1904)
teaser: Monet painting the same building at every hour of the day — smoke, fog and Thames light turning stone into colour. He painted nearly a hundred views of the Palace of Westminster from a hotel balcony. Each canvas is the same building and a different atmosphere; the series was about light, never architecture.

exploreAction.targetName: The Houses of Parliament series (1904) light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the building dissolves into the sky — for Monet the stone and the fog are the same material. Then compare two paintings of the same view: the difference is the light, and nothing else.

name: The Japanese Bridge (1899)
teaser: The green footbridge over Monet's lily pond at Giverny, painted from the water's edge — the view that became his obsession for thirty years. The bridge appears in dozens of versions as his sight failed and the pond became abstract. This early version is still recognizably a bridge in a garden; the later ones are pure colour.

exploreAction.targetName: The Japanese Bridge (1899) reflections
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the arch reflected in the water — the pond doubles the bridge. Then notice the willows and irises: this is the garden Monet built to paint.

name: Poppies (1873)
teaser: A field of red poppies in two quick bands of colour, with a woman and child walking through — a summer afternoon reduced to its essence. Monet painted the poppies as scattered red dabs, not flowers; the field reads as a staccato rhythm. It is one of the most reproduced of all Impressionist images.

exploreAction.targetName: Poppies (1873) red dabs
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the poppies are painted — dabs of red, not petals. Then find the second pair of walkers on the hill: the painting contains the same figures twice.

name: The Seine at Argenteuil (1874)
teaser: Sailing boats on the Seine at the village where Monet kept a studio — the river as a mirror of sky, painted in the summer light he loved. Monet lived at Argenteuil for seven years and painted its bridges, boats and banks obsessively. The water here is almost pure reflection; the boats float on sky.

exploreAction.targetName: The Seine at Argenteuil (1874) reflections
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water — it is painted as horizontal strokes of sky-colour, not wetness. Then notice the rowing boat and the sail: leisure is the subject, and the light is the real content.

name: Bordighera (1884)
teaser: Palm trees and Mediterranean light on the Italian Riviera — Monet's escape from the grey winter of Giverny, painted in a single visit. The palms were a new subject and he wrestled with them, calling the light 'barbarous'. The result is a painting of heat: the sea, the palms and the walls all tremble in the same glare.

exploreAction.targetName: Bordighera (1884) light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the palms — Monet complained he couldn't paint them, then made them the whole picture. The heat is almost visible: the colours vibrate against each other.

name: The Woman in the Garden (1867)
teaser: A woman in a white dress turning in a sunlit garden, her skirt catching the light — painted outdoors with a trench dug in the lawn so Monet could paint the full figure without changing his viewpoint. The light through the leaves breaks the white dress into coloured patches. It was rejected by the Salon, which was Monet's first taste of the battle to come.

exploreAction.targetName: The Woman in the Garden (1867) light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the white dress — it is really made of colour: green shadows, yellow sun, blue sky. Then imagine the trench: Monet literally dug to keep his sightline.

name: The Swing (1876)
teaser: A woman on a garden swing, her dress flying, watched by two men in the shade — a moment of pure flirtation in dappled light. Renoir painted the light falling through leaves as loose strokes of colour that dissolve the scene. The swing's motion is implied by the dress and the shadow; the picture seems to move as you look.

exploreAction.targetName: The Swing (1876) dappled light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light patches across the dress and the ground — Renoir's brush breaks the garden into colour. Then find the little girl watching from the left: an audience inside the painting.

name: The Dance at Bougival (1883)
teaser: A couple dancing at an open-air café — she in a red dress tilted back in his arms, he with his hat tipped forward. The woman is Suzanne Valadon, who would become a painter herself. Renoir painted three large dance pictures that year; this one is the most intimate, the couple locked mid-turn.

exploreAction.targetName: The Dance at Bougival (1883) the couple
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman's face — tilted up, eyes half-closed, completely trusting the turn. Then notice the background: the dance floor is a blur of other couples, and the two of them are the only clear figures.

name: The Umbrellas (1885)
teaser: A crowd of Parisians under umbrellas in a rain shower — painted over several years, in two different styles: the right side is crisp and linear, the left softer and more Impressionist. Renoir abandoned the canvas midway and returned to it later, and the two halves betray the gap. The little girl with the hoop is his future wife's sister.

exploreAction.targetName: The Umbrellas (1885) two styles
exploreAction.instruction: Look for the seam — the right side of the canvas is tighter, the left looser, painted years apart. Then find the girl with the hoop: she's looking straight at us, the only figure who does.

name: La Goulue arriving at the Moulin Rouge (1892)
teaser: The queen of the can-can sweeping into the Moulin Rouge with her sister, her chin up, the crowd parting — painted by the aristocrat dwarf who lived among the dancers. Toulouse-Lautrec's poster of La Goulue made her and him famous. This painting shows the star offstage, still performing.

exploreAction.targetName: La Goulue arriving at the Moulin Rouge (1892) entrance
exploreAction.instruction: Look at La Goulue's chin — held high, expecting the room to notice. Then look at the faces around her: Lautrec painted his friends as a gallery of Paris nightlife.

name: Jane Avril (1893)
teaser: The dancer Jane Avril in a black dress and feathered hat, her profile sharp against a yellow wall — a poster made for her cabaret appearances that became an icon of the Belle Époque. Lautrec painted the dancer who became his close friend dozens of times. This poster's bold flat shapes made it a landmark of graphic design.

exploreAction.targetName: Jane Avril (1893) poster
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flat shapes — the yellow wall, the black dress, the red hair: no shading, pure silhouette. Then notice the bassist's neck and scroll at the bottom: the music is folded into the design.

name: Dancer Adjusting Her Shoe (1890)
teaser: A ballerina bending to fix her slipper, caught mid-movement in pastel — the unglamorous moment Degas made his subject. The pastel lets the figure dissolve at the edges, as if glimpsed in motion. The pose is awkward, almost painful; that's the point. The ballet's beauty, Degas insisted, was in its effort.

exploreAction.targetName: Dancer Adjusting Her Shoe (1890) pastel
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the figure's edges — the pastel dissolves the outline so the dancer seems to be moving. Then notice the effort in the pose: Degas painted the work, not the glamour, of ballet.

name: The Basket of Apples (1893)
teaser: A tilted basket of apples, a bottle, a cloth — the most famous still life in the history of still life, where the tabletop itself refuses to lie flat. Cézanne's apples are painted as volumes, not fruits, and the perspective shifts between objects on purpose. He said he wanted to 'astonish Paris with an apple'.

exploreAction.targetName: The Basket of Apples (1893) perspective
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the table's edges — they don't line up, because Cézanne painted each object from a slightly different angle. The apples are the true subject: solid, round, almost touchable.

name: The Boy in the Red Vest (1889)
teaser: A boy in a scarlet waistcoat leaning on his elbow — painted four times, each version turning the same pose into a different rhythm of colour and space. The red vest against the grey-blue background is Cézanne's purest colour experiment. The boy's name is unknown; he was a model, paid to hold a pose Cézanne couldn't stop painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Boy in the Red Vest (1889) the red
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the red vest — it's the only bright colour in the painting, and the whole composition orbits it. Then notice the pose: the boy's twisted body gives the flat picture its depth.

name: Jug and Fruit (1894)
teaser: A jug, a fruit dish and a crumpled cloth on a table — Cézanne's lifelong subject, painted as a study in volumes and the spaces between them. The objects are solid, the cloth is a landscape of folds. Cézanne made the still life his laboratory: 'I will astonish Paris with an apple', he said, and he did.

exploreAction.targetName: Jug and Fruit (1894) volumes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the jug's symmetry against the cloth's chaos — Cézanne set the two against each other. Then notice how the fruit is painted as pure volume: spheres, not apples.

name: The Three Musicians (1921)
teaser: Three masked musicians — a harlequin, a pierrot and a monk — cut from flat planes of colour, painted in Picasso's synthetic Cubist style. The figures collapse into the picture plane yet hold together like a band mid-song. Picasso painted two versions in the same year, one in Philadelphia, one at MoMA, and both are considered masterpieces.

exploreAction.targetName: The Three Musicians (1921) flat planes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the three figures interlock — the shapes share edges, so the group reads as one cut-out. Then find the dog under the table: a sliver of Cubist humour in the pattern.

name: Weeping Woman (1937)
teaser: A woman sobbing, her face broken into sharp planes, her handkerchief pressed to her teeth — Picasso's image of grief distilled into geometry. Painted in the same year as Guernica, it belongs to the same series of suffering. The subject is Dora Maar, the photographer who documented Guernica's creation. Picasso painted her weeping again and again; she said he never painted her smiling.

exploreAction.targetName: Weeping Woman (1937) the face
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the tears — painted as sharp shards of blue and white, not soft drops. Then notice the teeth and the handkerchief: grief here is a machine of angles.

name: Portrait of Dora Maar (1937)
teaser: Dora Maar, photographer, Surrealist and Picasso's companion, painted as a queen of angles — her profile split, her face both profile and front view at once. The portrait turns a real person into a diagram of looking. Maar photographed the making of Guernica, then Picasso's portraits of her grew increasingly distorted as their relationship soured.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of Dora Maar (1937) double profile
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the face — you see it from two sides at once, which is impossible and utterly convincing. Then notice the painted nail: one detail of the real woman survives the geometry.

name: Girl with a Mandolin (1910)
teaser: A figure dissolved into a lattice of facets — the painting that pushed Cubism to its limit, where the girl and her mandolin are almost unrecognizable. Only the instrument's sound-hole keeps the subject readable. Picasso said he wanted to paint 'not the girl, but the angles'. The background and figure share the same planes.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl with a Mandolin (1910) facets
exploreAction.instruction: Look for the mandolin's sound-hole — the single curve that anchors the whole lattice. Then notice how the background and the figure are built from the same shapes: space and body are one material.

name: Puberty (1894)
teaser: A naked girl on the edge of a bed, her hands clasped over herself, a shadow looming behind her — one of the most uncomfortable paintings in art. Munch painted the moment between childhood and the world's expectations. The shadow is the future; the girl's stare is the present. It was banned, burned and censored for decades.

exploreAction.targetName: Puberty (1894) the shadow
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the shadow — it looms where the bed ends, bigger than the girl. Then look at her hands: clasped, guarded, the only defence in the room. Munch painted anxiety before it had a name.

name: The Kiss (1897)
