teaser: Two figures fused into one dark mass, their faces melting together in a kiss — Munch's image of love as merger and loss of self. Unlike Klimt's glittering embrace, this kiss erases identity: the two heads become a single shape. Munch painted it repeatedly, each version darker. It is love seen from the inside of a panic attack.

exploreAction.targetName: The Kiss (1897) the fusion
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faces — they have no features left, just two silhouettes become one. Then notice the room: bare, dark, closing in. For Munch, the kiss was also a disappearing.

name: Death and Life (1915)
teaser: A column of sleeping figures — mothers, lovers, children — facing a grinning skeleton wrapped in fabric. Klimt painted the figures as a cascade of pattern and flesh, the death as a cold cartoon. He reworked the painting in 1915, adding the grey background that isolates the two halves. It is his meditation on the one subject he couldn't gild.

exploreAction.targetName: Death and Life (1915) the two halves
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the skeleton — flat, patterned, almost an ornament, while the bodies are full of pattern and colour. Then notice the empty gap between them: the two sides never touch.

name: The Three Ages of Woman (1905)
teaser: A child, a woman and an old woman in a single composition of flesh and ornament — childhood glowing, maturity flowering, age folding in on itself. Klimt painted the three ages as one continuous body of work, and the old woman's despair is deliberately unsparing. It won the gold medal at the 1911 International Exhibition in Rome.

exploreAction.targetName: The Three Ages of Woman (1905) the old woman
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the old woman — she covers her face while the other two glow. Then notice the ornament: the younger figures are wrapped in Klimt's pattern, the oldest stripped bare of it.

name: Adele Bloch-Bauer II (1912)
teaser: Adele Bloch-Bauer a second time — standing in a green gown against a garden of colour, a softer and more modern portrait than the gold-leaf first version. Painted four years apart, the two portraits show the same woman through Klimt's changing style. It sold for $87.9 million in 2006, hours after the gold portrait set the record.

exploreAction.targetName: Adele Bloch-Bauer II (1912) colour
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the background — a mosaic of greens, pinks and blues that turns the wall into a garden. Then compare the two portraits: this Adele stands in colour where the first sits in gold.

name: The Beethoven Frieze (1902)
teaser: A 34-metre mural painted for an exhibition celebrating Beethoven — a wall-length allegory of humanity's struggle toward joy, ending with a kiss that has become one of Klimt's most reproduced images. The frieze was meant to be temporary; it was rescued, cut into sections and reassembled. The 'kiss' at the end is the embrace of the whole world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Beethoven Frieze (1902) the final kiss
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sequence: suffering, longing, then the final embrace. The figures are painted flat with gold and mother-of-pearl, like a page from a giant illuminated manuscript.

name: Hope II (1908)
teaser: A pregnant woman in a patterned robe, her hands pressed to her belly, three figures at her feet — painted the same year a scandal greeted Klimt's first 'Hope' painting, which showed a nude pregnant woman. This version wraps her in gold and pattern, the pregnancy abstracted into ornament. It is one of the few major paintings of pregnancy in Western art.

exploreAction.targetName: Hope II (1908) the robe
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the robe — the pattern draws the eye to the belly like a map. Then look at her hands: folded over the child, the composition's true centre.

name: The Annunciation (1434)
teaser: The angel Gabriel and Mary in a church so detailed you can read the stained glass — van Eyck's oil technique let him paint light through windows, shadows on marble, and the words of the angel's greeting painted upside-down as if spoken into the air. The church is a metaphor: the New Testament arriving inside the Old.

exploreAction.targetName: The Annunciation (1434) details
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the painted words — Gabriel's greeting appears upside-down on the canvas, as if flying from his mouth. Then find the seven windows: the light is theology made paint.

name: The Descent from the Cross (1435)
teaser: Christ's body lowered from the cross in a composition so tight that every figure seems pressed together by grief — Mary swooning in the same arc as her son, the shroud held like a cradle. Van der Weyden compressed the scene into a shallow stage, making the sorrow feel immediate. It became the most copied painting in the north.

exploreAction.targetName: The Descent from the Cross (1435) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the curve of Mary's body — it mirrors Christ's, grief repeating his form. Then notice the shallow space: the figures are packed like a relief, emotion at full pressure.

name: Portrait of a Lady (1460)
teaser: An unknown woman, hands folded like a closed book, her veil framing a face of unnerving stillness — the most famous anonymous portrait of the 1400s. The downward sweep of her eyelid and the corner of her mouth make her look at once serene and sorrowful. Her identity is lost; her presence is not.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of a Lady (1460) the veil
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the hands — pressed together as if holding something invisible. Then look at the veil's geometry: every fold is drawn with the precision of a map.

name: The Mérode Altarpiece (1427)
teaser: The Annunciation in a Flemish burgher's home — Mary reading in a tidy room, Gabriel arriving through the window, Joseph working at his carpentry bench. Campin painted the holy event as ordinary household life, full of coded objects: the extinguished candle, the lilies, the mousetrap (a symbol of Christ catching the devil). One of the earliest oil paintings to survive.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mérode Altarpiece (1427) symbols
exploreAction.instruction: Look for the mousetrap on Joseph's bench — Campin's inside joke about God baiting the devil. Then notice the town through the window: the everyday world pressed against the sacred room.

name: The Battle of San Romano (1438)
teaser: Florentine cavalry clashing in a forest of lances — Uccello's celebration of perspective, painted as a decorative frieze of armoured knights and fallen horses. The lances are laid out like a geometry exercise, and the horses rear in frozen theatrical poses. Uccello was famously obsessed with perspective; his wife reportedly called him to bed each night saying 'the perspective is in bed'. The painting was once a single triptych; its panels now live in three museums.

exploreAction.targetName: The Battle of San Romano (1438) lances
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lances — they radiate like a compass, Uccello showing off his mastery of foreshortening. Then notice the fallen soldier's foreshortened body on the ground: perspective as battlefield.

name: The Tribute Money (1425)
teaser: Christ, the tax collector and Peter in a single continuous scene — the moment Christ tells Peter to find a coin in a fish's mouth, told in three sequential moments within one fresco. Masaccio's breakthrough was light: one consistent source casting real shadows, making the figures solid for the first time in a century. It is the painting that started the Renaissance.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tribute Money (1425) light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the shadows — every figure casts a consistent shadow from the same light, a shock in 1425. Then follow Peter's journey: the same apostle appears three times in one scene.

name: The Mystical Nativity (1501)
teaser: The birth of Christ watched by angels, shepherds and demons — painted in a year Botticelli believed was the end of the world. Three angels embrace three men at the bottom, the saved and the damned reconciled. The Greek inscription at the top warns of tribulation and names the painter's hopes. It is Botticelli's last great painting and his strangest.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mystical Nativity (1501) inscription
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the angels at the bottom — they embrace humans under the olive boughs, a reconciliation Botticelli desperately hoped for. Then read the inscription: it predicts the end of the world in 1501.

name: Venus and Mars (1485)
teaser: Venus watching over the sleeping god of war while satyrs play with his armour — the goddess of love has conquered war, who sleeps it off. Mars is sprawled in an impossible pose, his helmet and lance stolen by tiny satyrs. The panel was a wedding gift: a promise that love tames violence. Botticelli painted it with a wink.

exploreAction.targetName: Venus and Mars (1485) the satyrs
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Mars's pose — utterly defenceless, snoring while his weapons are played with. Then find the satyr blowing a conch in his ear: the god of war sleeps through it all.

name: The Sistine Madonna (1512)
teaser: Mary carrying the Christ child down to earth, flanked by saints, with the two famous cherubs leaning on the frame's edge below. The curtain has opened; the Madonna steps into our world. The bottom pair of angels became the most reproduced cherubs in history — they're on posters, mugs and banknotes. The painting is Raphael's last Madonna and his most tender.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sistine Madonna (1512) the cherubs
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two cherubs at the bottom — borrowed from a real sketch Raphael made of a boy in the street. Then look at Mary's bare feet: she has stepped off her heavenly cloud onto the world's floor.

name: Lady with an Ermine (1490)
teaser: Cecilia Gallerani holding an ermine — the animal of the Sforza family and a symbol of purity — with her hand and the creature's body turning in the same elegant spiral. Leonardo painted the ermine as a living animal, alert and twisting, a study of movement decades before motion studies. It is one of only four portraits of women by Leonardo.

exploreAction.targetName: Lady with an Ermine (1490) the ermine
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the spiral of the pose — the woman, the ermine and her hand all turn together. Then notice the animal's alertness: Leonardo painted it mid-movement, not as a prop.

name: Ginevra de' Benci (1478)
teaser: A young Florentine woman in a portrait that was revolutionary for its inwardness — she is beautiful but not posed for admiration; her face is pale, her gaze averted, her personality closed. Leonardo painted her against a juniper bush (ginevra plays on ginepro, juniper) and used the new oil technique to model her face with soft shadow. It is the only Leonardo painting in the Americas.

exploreAction.targetName: Ginevra de' Benci (1478) the gaze
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her face — Leonardo modelled it with shadow, not outline, so she seems present rather than posed. Then find the juniper behind her: a botanical pun on her name.

name: The Last Judgment (1541)
teaser: The end of the world painted across the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel — a whirlwind of resurrected bodies, saints and demons, with Christ at the centre raising his hand. It scandalized the Church: naked bodies, a saint with a trophy skin, and the Pope's master of ceremonies depicted as a serpent-bitten fool. Michelangelo painted it twenty years after the ceiling, angrier and more monumental.

exploreAction.targetName: The Last Judgment (1541) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Christ's raised arm — the whole composition spins around it like a storm. Then find Saint Bartholomew holding his flayed skin: the face on the skin is Michelangelo's own self-portrait.

name: View of Toledo (1600)
teaser: The Spanish city of Toledo under a sky of boiling silver — painted not as a map but as a mood, with the cathedral and the Alcázar looming over the gorge. El Greco rearranged the city's actual geography for drama: buildings move, the sky is a storm of light. It is one of the first great landscape paintings in European art, and it shows a place as a vision.

exploreAction.targetName: View of Toledo (1600) the sky
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky — silver, green and black, more powerful than the city. Then notice the geography is invented: El Greco moved real buildings to make a truer portrait of the place's mood.

name: The Burial of the Count of Orgaz (1586)
teaser: Heaven opening over a funeral: saints lowering the dead count into his tomb while angels carry his soul upward — the earthly scene painted with precise portraits, the heavenly half dissolving into flame and light. El Greco signed his name on a handkerchief in the crowd. The painting split into two worlds, and both are masterpieces.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burial of the Count of Orgaz (1586) two halves
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the boundary between earth and heaven — the saints are solid, the sky is pure light. Then find the boy at the left pointing at the miracle: he is the painter's son, and his handkerchief carries El Greco's signature.

name: Woman in Blue Reading a Letter (1663)
teaser: A pregnant woman reading a letter by a window, the map on the wall behind her hinting at an absent husband — Vermeer's most intimate study of a private moment. The blue of her jacket is ultramarine, the most expensive pigment of the age. The light falls on the letter, not her face: the message is the subject.

exploreAction.targetName: Woman in Blue Reading a Letter (1663) the letter
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light on the letter — the only bright surface in the room. Then notice the map: Vermeer painted it with the creases of a real map, a clue to the letter's subject.

name: The Music Lesson (1665)
teaser: A young woman at a virginal watched by her teacher, the mirror above them reflecting the room — including the painter's own easel. Vermeer's obsession with optics fills the scene: the mirror, the perspective, the light through the window. The virginal's lid carries an inscription: 'Music is the companion of joy, the healer of sorrow.'

exploreAction.targetName: The Music Lesson (1665) the mirror
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mirror — it reflects the woman's face AND the artist's easel, a self-portrait hidden in plain sight. Then read the virginal's lid: the motto explains the room.

name: Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window (1657)
teaser: A girl reading by an open window, her reflection barely visible in the glass — one of Vermeer's earliest interiors and his first essay in the theme of letters and longing. X-rays revealed that the wall behind her originally held a large painting of Cupid, painted over by the artist or another hand. The window's light is the real subject.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window (1657) the glass
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the window — the glass is a mirror so faint you almost miss the girl's reflection. Then know the secret: X-rays show a Cupid was once on the wall behind her, a love story painted out.

name: The Embarkation for Cythera (1717)
teaser: Couples preparing to board a golden boat for the island of love — the painting that invented the fête galante, a genre of dreamy aristocratic courtship. Watteau's lovers hesitate rather than depart; the whole scene is a sigh in paint. It made his name at the French Academy, which had to invent a new category for it.

exploreAction.targetName: The Embarkation for Cythera (1717) the couples
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the couples — they're turning back, reluctant to leave. Then notice the statue of Venus and the cupids: the island of love is decorated for a departure that never quite happens.

name: The Ray (1728)
teaser: A gutted ray hanging over a kitchen table of fish, jugs and a cat — a still life so honest that it made Chardin's reputation overnight. The ray's pale underside glows like a strange flower; the composition is a quiet masterpiece of shapes. Diderot called Chardin 'the great magician'. A still life was never just still life again.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ray (1728) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the ray's underside — it reads almost like a creature from a dream. Then notice the cat and the oyster: Chardin's kitchen is a theatre of textures.

name: Soap Bubbles (1734)
teaser: A boy blowing a soap bubble through a straw while another watches — an everyday moment with an old moral: life is brief, like the bubble. Chardin painted the boy with his back to us, so the bubble's fragility is the subject. The painting's stillness makes the bubble's imminent pop almost audible. It was a favourite of Enlightenment thinkers.

exploreAction.targetName: Soap Bubbles (1734) the bubble
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the bubble — a perfect sphere of light about to vanish. Then notice the boy's absorption: the whole painting is the second before the pop.

name: The Turkish Bath (1862)
teaser: A circle of nude women in a Turkish bath — painted by Ingres in his eighties, a lifetime of odalisques condensed into one ring of flesh. The composition is a perfect circle, the figures pressed together like a mosaic. It scandalized and fascinated Paris; Ingres kept it in his studio for years, adjusting figures even into his eighties. The arched window at the back opens onto nothing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Turkish Bath (1862) the circle
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the circular composition — every figure flows into the next, a wreath of bodies. Then find the bather at the back playing a lute: she is a quote from Ingres's own earlier painting.

name: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters (1799)
teaser: A sleeping man slumped over a desk while owls and bats swarm around him — the frontispiece of Goya's Caprichos, his series of satirical prints attacking superstition and folly. The title cuts both ways: reason asleep breeds monsters, but so does reason's confidence. The etching is the manifesto of the modern artist as social critic.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters (1799) the owls
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the owl at the desk — it offers a pen, inviting the dreamer to keep writing. Then read the image both ways: the monsters are born of sleep, but also of the awake world's foolishness.

name: Garden at Sainte-Adresse (1867)
teaser: A seaside garden in bright diagonal sunlight — four figures on a terrace, the Channel behind them, a flag catching the wind. Monet painted it from his aunt's house with the sea and the sky as a backdrop. The composition is built from bold diagonals, and the painting already shows the flat colour areas that would become his style. It was a hit at the 1867 Salon, one of his first.

exploreAction.targetName: Garden at Sainte-Adresse (1867) diagonals
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flag and the boat smoke — the only moving things in a painting of stillness. Then notice the composition: Monet built the whole scene on diagonals, a decade before his famous series.

name: The Gare Saint-Lazare series (1877)
teaser: The glass-roofed train station in Paris painted from inside the smoke — twelve canvases of locomotives, steam and soot that made the modern city a fit subject for art. Monet wore his best clothes and asked the station master to hold the trains so the steam would be right. The smoke turns the shed into a cathedral of cloud.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gare Saint-Lazare series (1877) smoke
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the steam — it fills the glass roof like weather, the trains emerging from it like ghosts. Then picture Monet in his Sunday suit, persuading railwaymen to stage his scenes.

name: The Box (1874)
teaser: A couple in a theatre box, she in pearls leaning forward, he in evening dress looking through opera glasses — the Parisian leisure class at its most glamorous. The woman is the painter's future model; the scene is about seeing and being seen. Renoir painted the box with the looseness of a sketch, the opera glasses catching the light.

exploreAction.targetName: The Box (1874) the audience
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman's pearls and the man's glasses — the painting is a study in looking. Then notice the blurred audience behind: Renoir painted the social game of who watches whom.

name: The Bellelli Family (1867)
teaser: Degas's aunt, uncle and two cousins in a sombre salon — a family portrait with the tension left in. The mother stands in black, the father sits half-turned away, the girls keep a careful distance. Degas painted it in Florence over two years, and the psychology is as sharp as the drawing. It is his first masterpiece and his most intimate.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bellelli Family (1867) the tension
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the space between the parents — the father is turned away, the mother stands apart. Then look at the girls: they mirror the divide. Degas painted the family's fault line with perfect manners.

name: The Star (1878)
teaser: A ballerina on stage caught in the footlights, arms raised mid-bow, while the corps dissolves in the wings — Degas's image of the dancer as both star and silhouette. The pastel technique lets the light flare around her like a halo. It is the moment of triumph, and also the moment the star is alone on stage.

exploreAction.targetName: The Star (1878) the light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the footlights — they flare through the pastel like a flash. Then look at the wings: the star is the only clear figure, everything else dissolving into the dark.

name: The Tub (1886)
teaser: A woman sponging herself in a metal tub, seen from above at a startling angle — the bather as seen by nobody, unposed and unguarded. Degas's late pastels of women washing were criticized as ugly; he called them 'the nude, viewed from the keyhole'. The composition is radical: the tub's rim crosses the canvas, and the figure is off-centre.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tub (1886) the angle
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the viewpoint — from above and off-centre, as if the painter is not supposed to be there. Then notice the metal tub's reflection: Degas painted the water and the room in its curved surface.

name: Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose (1886)
teaser: Two little girls lighting paper lanterns in an English garden at dusk — the title from a popular song, the light a miracle of timing. Sargent painted it for two summers, working only in the final minutes of daylight when the lanterns' glow balanced the fading sky. The girls stood motionless for minutes at a time while he worked. It is his most loved painting.

exploreAction.targetName: Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose (1886) the light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the glow — the lanterns and the dusk are painted to the same brightness, which only happens for about twenty minutes. Then know the method: Sargent repainted it all the next summer, chasing the same minute of light.

name: The Swimming Hole (1885)
teaser: Nude young men at a swimming hole, posed with the geometry of a frieze — Eakins's study of the body in motion and sunlight, painted from photographs he staged himself. The figures are arranged like a classical relief, but the setting is an ordinary American river. The painting scandalized Philadelphia's art establishment, and Eakins's reputation suffered for his honesty about the body.

exploreAction.targetName: The Swimming Hole (1885) composition
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the arrangement — the swimmers are placed like figures on a Greek frieze. Then know the method: Eakins posed his friends for photographs first, then painted the bodies with anatomical precision.

name: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878)
teaser: A small girl slouched in an oversized blue armchair, legs out, mind elsewhere — a child painted without sentimentality. Cassatt, the American who joined the Impressionists, made the sitter her friend's daughter. The loose armchair and the tilted floor show Degas's influence; he suggested the background. It is childhood as it is, not as adults imagine it.

exploreAction.targetName: Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878) the pose
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the girl's pose — slumped, bored, utterly real. Then notice the armchair's size: the furniture is the adult world, and she is lost in it.

name: Broadway Boogie Woogie (1942)
teaser: New York City reduced to its grid — a map of Manhattan's streets as coloured blocks and lines, painted by the Dutch artist who fled the war and fell in love with the city's rhythm. The tiny coloured squares are traffic and jazz. Mondrian considered it his masterpiece; he worked on it until his death two years later. It is his farewell to Europe and his hello to America.

exploreAction.targetName: Broadway Boogie Woogie (1942) the grid
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the yellow lines — they run like taxi routes through the grid. Then find the clusters of coloured blocks: Mondrian said the painting was jazz you could see.

name: Early Sunday Morning (1930)
teaser: A row of empty shopfronts on a silent street — no people, no traffic, just a barber pole, a fire hydrant and long morning shadows. Hopper's city is always waiting for something that doesn't arrive. The light is the only character: it falls on the buildings like a question. It is the definitive image of American solitude.

exploreAction.targetName: Early Sunday Morning (1930) the emptiness
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the windows — every one is dark, every shop closed. Then notice the barber pole: the only colour in the street, spinning nowhere. Hopper called it 'almost a street scene'.

name: Autumn Rhythm (1950)
teaser: A 5-metre tangle of black, white and rust paint — Pollock's poured-paint method at full scale, the canvas laid on the floor and attacked from all sides. The title came after the painting, when the skeins read like autumn wind. It is the purest statement of action painting: the painting is the record of the movement that made it.

exploreAction.targetName: Autumn Rhythm (1950) the weave
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the layers — black lines over white lines over rust, a woven surface with real depth. Then step back: the chaos resolves into a rhythm, which is what the title claims.

name: The Great Masturbator (1929)
teaser: A giant distorted head in a desert landscape — nose on the ground, a grasshopper clinging to its mouth, a woman's face emerging from its skull — Dalí's most personal painting, made at the height of his fame. The title is deliberate provocation; the imagery is about desire, fear and his own psyche. It is the painting that made Surrealism's most notorious artist.

exploreAction.targetName: The Great Masturbator (1929) symbols
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman's face inside the head — desire embedded in the skull. Then find the grasshopper: Dalí was terrified of them, and painted his fear in.

name: The Disquieting Muses (1917)
teaser: Two mannequin-like figures and a classical statue in a shadowed piazza — the unsettling stillness that founded Metaphysical painting, the movement Surrealism grew out of. De Chirico's empty squares and faceless figures made ordinary architecture feel haunted. The title says it: the muses are here, and they are not comforting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Disquieting Muses (1917) the mannequins
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faceless figures — bodies without heads, heads without faces. Then notice the shadow: long, wrong, from a sun that isn't in the painting.

name: The Elephant Celebes (1921)
teaser: A huge mechanical elephant — part boiler, part beast — squatting in a strange room, a headless mannequin reaching toward it. Ernst built it from a photograph of a Sudanese grain store, collaged and repainted into a monster. It is the first great painting of Surrealism, made before the movement had its name.

exploreAction.targetName: The Elephant Celebes (1921) the creature
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the creature's trunk — it's a hose, not a nose. Then notice the room: no floor, no sense of scale, everything built to unsettle.

name: The Birth of the World (1925)
teaser: A field of abstract colour — red sky, blue ground, a black triangle, a drifting star and a single line — Miró's vision of creation as pure chance. He made it by letting paint drip and pool, then adding the few decisive signs. It is the painting where his style was born: few elements, infinite space.

exploreAction.targetName: The Birth of the World (1925) the signs
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the bare canvas showing through — Miró left most of it empty, which is the point. Then find the star and the triangle: two signs in a universe of nothing.

name: Over the Town (1918)
teaser: A man and woman flying over their hometown — the painter himself and his bride Bella, floating above the rooftops of Vitebsk. Chagall painted love as a physical force: gravity gives up. The little village below, the fiddler on the roof, the upside-down lovers — it is the happiest painting in the history of art.

exploreAction.targetName: Over the Town (1918) the lovers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lovers — they float without wings, held up by nothing but each other. Then notice the town below: Chagall kept flying back to it in paint for the rest of his life.

name: Improvisation 28 (1912)
teaser: A storm of colour and line that Kandinsky called 'the inner sound' — painted before abstract art had a name, when he was still calling his pictures improvisations on a theme. Hidden in the swirl are a charging horseman and cannons, echoes of the war coming. It is the moment painting began to let go of the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Improvisation 28 (1912) the forms
exploreAction.instruction: Look for the shapes — a rider, a cannon, a tower, all dissolving into colour. Then step back: the picture works as pure music, which is what Kandinsky wanted.

name: Ad Parnassum (1932)
teaser: A mountain of mosaic squares — thousands of tiny rectangles building a sun and a peak, painted after Klee visited Egypt and was dazzled by its light. The title means 'to Parnassus', the mountain of the muses. It is Klee's most famous painting and his most pointillist: the whole picture vibrates like a mosaic seen through heat.

exploreAction.targetName: Ad Parnassum (1932) the mosaic
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the squares — every one is a decision, thousands of them building the mountain. Then find the sun: it glows through the grid like a window.

name: The Newborn (1915)
teaser: A baby's head reduced to a polished oval with a single line for a mouth — Brancusi's sculpture of the first breath of life, so simplified it is almost abstract. The mouth is open, mid-cry or mid-dream. Brancusi polished his bronzes to a mirror finish because he wanted light to be part of the form. It is one of the most tender objects in modern art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Newborn (1915) the form
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the head — an egg with a mouth, nothing more, and somehow a whole baby. Then notice the shine: Brancusi polished it so the light itself becomes the skin.

name: Sleeping Muse (1910)
teaser: An oval head on a tilted plane, eyes closed, features barely marked — Brancusi's first great sculpture and the beginning of his lifelong obsession with the head as an egg. The muse sleeps with her face half-erased, like a memory of a face. It is stillness made solid.

exploreAction.targetName: Sleeping Muse (1910) the profile
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the profile — the features are nearly gone, reduced to a few lines. Then notice the tilt of the head: the whole sculpture is a single pose of rest.

name: King and Queen (1953)
teaser: A seated king and queen in bronze, their heads hollowed into crowns and profiles — royalty reduced to monumental simplicity. Moore made the pair with the holes and hollows that became his signature, spaces that make the sculpture belong to the landscape around it. The king and queen sit forever, looking out over the hills.

exploreAction.targetName: King and Queen (1953) the hollows
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the heads — hollowed out, so the sky shows through the crowns. Then notice the pose: seated, patient, monumental, built for an open field.

name: Single Form (1963)
teaser: A towering bronze abstract in the United Nations plaza — Hepworth's memorial to Dag Hammarskjöld, the UN Secretary-General who died in a plane crash. The form suggests a figure, a flame, a prayer. Hepworth said it was about 'the single form of man' against the world. It stands in New York, an abstract monument to peace.

exploreAction.targetName: Single Form (1963) the silhouette
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the silhouette — it shifts as you walk, now figure, now flame, now void. Then know the occasion: Hepworth made it for a man who died trying to make peace.

name: Walking Man I (1961)
teaser: A gaunt, elongated figure striding forward — Giacometti's most famous sculpture, the image of humanity as a thin flame of existence. He worked for years trying to capture the figure as it is seen at a distance: stripped, uncertain, moving. A cast sold for $104 million in 2010, then the most expensive sculpture ever.

exploreAction.targetName: Walking Man I (1961) the stride
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the roughness — the bronze retains every thumbprint of the modelling. Then look at the stride: no muscle, no detail, just motion — the whole of a walk in one stride.

name: The Nose (1947)
teaser: A giant disembodied nose hanging in a cage, its long form pointing downward like a question — Giacometti's unsettling object, inspired by Gogol's story of a man who lost his nose. It is a head without a face, a face reduced to its most absurd feature. It hangs, it dangles, it refuses to be anything but itself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Nose (1947) the cage
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the cage — the nose is trapped, like a specimen. Then notice the length: Giacometti stretched it past anatomy into something comic and horrible at once.

name: Look Mickey (1961)
teaser: Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck at a fishing pond, Donald hooked by his own line — the painting that launched Pop Art, made from a children's book illustration and blown up to gallery scale. Lichtenstein painted the dots by hand, mimicking printing. The cartoon joke became the founding image of a movement.

exploreAction.targetName: Look Mickey (1961) the dots
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the dots — painted by hand, row after row, imitating a printing press. Then read Donald's panic: 'Look Mickey, I've hooked one!' — the caption makes it art about art.

name: Gold Marilyn Monroe (1962)
teaser: Marilyn Monroe's face in gold over a flat gold background, painted weeks after her death — Warhol's first Marilyn and his most solemn. The gold makes her an icon, a saint, a product. The face is printed from a publicity photo, the flaws of the print left in. It is the image of celebrity as religion.

exploreAction.targetName: Gold Marilyn Monroe (1962) the gold
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the gold field — it turns Marilyn into a Byzantine icon. Then notice the imperfect printing: Warhol left the smudges of the silkscreen in, because she was mass-produced too.

name: Target with Four Faces (1955)
teaser: A bullseye target painted in wax, four faces stacked above it in boxes, one covered by a flap — Johns's meditation on seeing and the things we look at without seeing. The target is a shape the mind completes instantly; the faces repeat it like a question. It made Johns the bridge between Abstract Expressionism and Pop.

exploreAction.targetName: Target with Four Faces (1955) the target
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the target — a thing so familiar you stop seeing it, which is Johns's point. Then notice the faces: identical, mute, and one hidden behind a flap you can't lift.

name: Canyon (1959)
teaser: A stuffed bald eagle, a pillow, a photograph, a street sign and oil paint fused into one object — Rauschenberg's 'combine', part painting, part sculpture. The eagle made the work illegal to sell (protected species), and for decades it could only be lent, never traded. It is the moment painting and sculpture gave up their separate rooms.

exploreAction.targetName: Canyon (1959) the combine
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eagle — real, stuffed, staring out of a painting. Then notice everything else: the pillow, the photo, the paint. Rauschenberg called these 'combines' because they refuse to choose a medium.

name: Study after Velázquez's Portrait of Pope Innocent X (1953)
teaser: The pope from Velázquez's portrait, screaming — his mouth torn open, his body dissolving into vertical brushstrokes, the golden throne turned into a cage of lines. Bacon painted the most famous portrait in history as a nightmare. He never saw the original, only reproductions; he said he was haunted by it.

exploreAction.targetName: Study after Velázquez's Portrait of Pope Innocent X (1953) the scream
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mouth — open in a scream that makes no sound, the cage of lines around it closing in. Then know: Bacon painted the same pope twenty times, each one a little more undone.

name: Girl with a White Dog (1952)
teaser: Freud's first wife lying on a bed, one hand on a white dog — painted with the thick, unflattering attention that made him the century's great portraitist of flesh. The pose is intimate and watchful at once. He painted her over many sittings, and the paint itself is like skin. It is the painting that announced his method.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl with a White Dog (1952) the flesh
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the paint — thick, worked, built like flesh rather than imitating it. Then notice the dog's gaze: it watches the viewer as steadily as the woman does.

name: Movement in Squares (1961)
teaser: A grid of black and white squares that seems to ripple and bulge — the painting that made Op Art a movement. Riley arranged identical squares and altered their spacing so the flat canvas appears to move, to breathe, to buckle. It is a painting that argues with your eyes and wins.

exploreAction.targetName: Movement in Squares (1961) the grid
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the grid — the squares are identical, only the gaps change, and the surface appears to swell. Then step back: the illusion holds, and that is the whole work.

name: Untitled #96 (1981)
teaser: A woman in a red sweater lying on a floor, clutching a personal ad from a newspaper — one of Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, photographs that mimic the look of 1950s movie publicity. The woman is Sherman herself, playing a character who is playing a role. It sold for $3.9 million in 2011, then the most expensive photograph ever.

exploreAction.targetName: Untitled #96 (1981) the pose
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman's expression — longing, staged, borrowed from a hundred forgotten films. Then notice the ad in her hand: the image is about women performing what they're told to want.

name: Child with Toy Hand Grenade in Central Park (1962)
teaser: A boy in the park, one hand clawed, the other holding a toy grenade — his face a mix of menace and plea. Arbus photographed strangers on the edge of the ordinary and found the strangeness in it. This is her most famous portrait, a child performing threat and helplessness at once. She said her subjects 'never told me a secret'.

exploreAction.targetName: Child with Toy Hand Grenade in Central Park (1962) the face
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the boy's face — both claws and begs. Then notice the background: an ordinary park, which makes the pose stranger, not less.

name: The Horse in Motion (1878)
teaser: The photograph that settled a bet: whether a galloping horse ever has all four hooves off the ground. Muybridge rigged twelve cameras along a track, each tripped by the horse's own motion, and the resulting sequence proved it — and invented motion pictures in the process. The bet was settled; cinema was born.

exploreAction.targetName: The Horse in Motion (1878) the sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the twelve frames — the answer to a centuries-old argument in a strip of images. Then notice what it made possible: every film ever made descends from this horse.

name: Dovima with Elephants (1955)
teaser: A model in a Dior evening gown posed between two circus elephants in Paris — the most famous fashion photograph ever taken, and the last day Dovima worked with Avedon. The elephants were borrowed from a circus; they were meant to be trained to pose, but Avedon just shot. The elegance of the dress against the grey hide is the whole image.

exploreAction.targetName: Dovima with Elephants (1955) the contrast
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the contrast — silk against hide, posture against bulk. Then know the story: the elephants weren't trained for the shot; Avedon improvised it in minutes, and it outlived every planned photograph.

name: Noire et Blanche (1926)
teaser: A model's face beside an African mask — two faces, one pale and one dark, one living and one carved, in near-identical profile. Man Ray's most famous photograph plays with resemblance and difference: the mask and the face are almost the same shape. The composition is pure geometry; the meanings are not.

exploreAction.targetName: Noire et Blanche (1926) the two faces
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two profiles — the mask and the face mirror each other so closely they seem to be one form split. Then notice the model's closed eyes: she is as still as the mask.

name: Hyères (1932)
teaser: A man cycling past a spiral staircase, the curved rail echoing his motion — the photograph that defined 'the decisive moment', Cartier-Bresson's phrase for catching reality at the instant it composes itself. He waited hours at this corner for the geometry to align. The bicycle, the spiral and the shadows lock into a single frozen chord.

exploreAction.targetName: Hyères (1932) the geometry
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the spiral staircase — the cyclist's curve rhymes with its curve, one motion in two materials. Then know the method: Cartier-Bresson called photography 'the decisive moment', and this is the proof.

name: Kiss by the Hôtel de Ville (1950)
teaser: A couple kissing on a busy Paris street, passers-by oblivious — the most famous kiss in photography, and the subject of a decades-long legal battle: the couple turned out to be hired models, and the photo was staged. Doisneau admitted it in 1992 when sued. The image remains the dream of Paris that the staging made real.

exploreAction.targetName: Kiss by the Hôtel de Ville (1950) the staging
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the kiss — set against the blur of the street, everyone else moving, the lovers frozen. Then know the twist: the lovers were models, hired by Doisneau, which made the dream a product.

name: Pepper No. 30 (1930)
teaser: A single green pepper photographed so closely it becomes a landscape of curves and shadows — Weston's most famous image, made in a tin funnel in his studio over many hours. He saw in the pepper 'the same forms as the human body'. The vegetable became monumental: folds like a torso, a hollow like a grotto.

exploreAction.targetName: Pepper No. 30 (1930) the forms
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the folds — the pepper reads as body, as mountain, as sculpture. Then know the setup: a tin funnel, a dark room, and hours of waiting for the light to be right.

name: The Snake Charmer (1907)
teaser: A dark-skinned flautist in a jungle at night, snakes writhing toward the music — painted by Rousseau, a customs clerk who never left France and painted his jungles from the botanical gardens and picture books. The moonlight, the black water and the hypnotic snakes make it his most mysterious work. Picasso bought it and kept it for life.

exploreAction.targetName: The Snake Charmer (1907) the jungle
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the moonlight — flat, green, dreamlike, like nothing on Earth. Then know the artist: Rousseau painted this jungle from Paris's botanical garden, and never saw a real snake charmer.

name: The Annunciation (San Marco)
teaser: The angel Gabriel kneels on a bare loggia and tells Mary she will bear God's son — painted in a monk's cell at San Marco, Florence, in cool pinks and blues. The light falls without a shadow, as if the message itself is the light. Fra Angelico believed painting was prayer; he prayed before he picked up the brush. The cell still holds it, 580 years on.

exploreAction.targetName: The Annunciation (San Marco) the quiet light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how quiet it is — no crowds, no gold, just two figures and a column of light. Then know Fra Angelico said painting was prayer, and he wept at the idea of Christ's suffering.

name: The Coronation of the Virgin
teaser: Christ crowns his mother while saints crowd a golden paradise — a panel of pure gold leaf and lapis blue, made for the church of Santa Maria Novella. Fra Angelico packed every inch with musicians, martyrs and angels in patterned robes. His nickname, 'the angelic brother', was earned by exactly this kind of luminous, humble joy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Coronation of the Virgin the golden paradise
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the saints — each one a real person with a face, a mood, a story. Then know Fra Angelico gave each halo a different gold pattern like a fingerprint.

name: The Adoration of the Magi
teaser: Three kings kneel before the infant Christ while the Medici family watches from the crowd — Botticelli painted his patrons into the Bible story, a bold move in 1475. The artist painted his own face at the far right, looking out at us. Cosimo de' Medici is said to be the magus kissing the baby's foot.

exploreAction.targetName: The Adoration of the Magi the self-portrait
exploreAction.instruction: Look right — the man in the ochre robe staring at us is Botticelli himself, the only time he painted his own face in a crowd scene.

name: Pallas and the Centaur
teaser: The goddess of wisdom holds a centaur's hair while he submits — a strange, dreamlike meeting of myth and mind, painted for Lorenzo de' Medici. No one agrees exactly what it means: temperance conquering lust, or reason taming instinct. The centaur's face is almost tender, like he's grateful to be led.

exploreAction.targetName: Pallas and the Centaur the submission
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the centaur's expression — he's not fighting, he's being calmed. Then know it was painted for Lorenzo de' Medici, whose emblem was the centaur.

name: The Calumny of Apelles
teaser: A king with donkey ears reaches toward Slander, who drags an innocent man by the hair while Truth stands naked at the far left — a painting about a painting. Botticelli rebuilt a lost Greek masterpiece by Apelles from a description by Lucian. It's his warning against false accusation, still painfully current.

exploreAction.targetName: The Calumny of Apelles the naked truth
exploreAction.instruction: Look left at the end — a naked woman pointing at the sky. That's Truth, ignored by everyone in the court, exactly as in the lost Greek original.

name: The Montefeltro Altarpiece
teaser: Mary sits enthroned in an egg-shaped apse while the duke of Urbino kneels in full armor — one of the most geometrically perfect paintings ever made. Piero was a mathematician; the egg above Mary's head is an ostrich egg, a symbol of the Immaculate Conception. The sleeping duke is Federico da Montefeltro, who lost his right eye in a tournament.

exploreAction.targetName: The Montefeltro Altarpiece the egg
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the ostrich egg hanging in the apse — an egg for the Immaculate Conception, placed by a painter who was also one of the great geometers of his age.

name: The Resurrection
teaser: Christ steps out of the tomb, one foot on the grave's edge, banner in hand, while Roman guards sleep below — a fresco that has been called the greatest painting in the world. The sleeping guards are alive with detail: one leans on his spear, one is folded into his own arms. Piero's Christ looks straight ahead, calm and absolutely certain.

exploreAction.targetName: The Resurrection the calm stare
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Christ's eyes — level, unblinking, straight at you. The guards below are dead asleep; the man above has already won. Aldous Huxley called it the greatest painting in the world.

name: Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione
teaser: The perfect courtier, painted by the perfect painter: grey eyes, soft beard, grey velvet — a study in understated intelligence. Castiglione wrote The Book of the Courtier, the manual of Renaissance manners. Raphael caught him mid-thought, a man whose whole profession was conversation.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of Baldassare Castiglione the grey eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eyes — grey, thoughtful, looking just past us. Then know this sitter wrote the book on how to be a Renaissance gentleman, and his friend Raphael painted the book's author.

name: Charles V at Mühlberg
teaser: The Holy Roman Emperor rides alone through a forest at dawn, lance raised, fresh from crushing the Protestant league — a portrait of absolute power on horseback. Titian painted the gout-ridden Charles as a knight in shining armor. The sky is still dark from the battle; the emperor is already past it.

exploreAction.targetName: Charles V at Mühlberg the lone rider
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how alone he is — no army, just a rider and a spear. Titian made the emperor look like destiny on horseback, and Charles reportedly kept the painting with him for the rest of his life.

name: The Disrobing of Christ
teaser: Christ looks calmly at us while a workman tears his red robe from him, the crowd surging in flame-like shapes — painted in Toledo, Spain, where El Greco made his home. The composition pushes the drama down below Christ's chest, so his face floats above the chaos. The red of the robe is the painting's heartbeat.

exploreAction.targetName: The Disrobing of Christ the red robe
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the robe — the reddest red in the painting, pulled from Christ while his face stays calm above the crowd. El Greco's figures seem to burn from inside.

name: The Opening of the Fifth Seal
teaser: Souls of the martyrs stretch upward in white flame, begging for justice, while the sky churns — an unfinished painting that inspired a century of modern art. The naked figures are elongated into pure emotion. Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon was born from staring at this canvas. It sat rolled up in a cellar for two hundred years.

exploreAction.targetName: The Opening of the Fifth Seal the white flames
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the figures — stretched, burning, reaching. Then know Picasso studied this exact canvas before painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, his own revolution.

name: Salome with the Head of John the Baptist
teaser: Salome holds the severed head of John the Baptist on a platter while a servant looks on — and the head is Caravaggio's own face. The artist painted his self-portrait as the dead prophet, a confession of guilt written in blood and shadow. He had been on the run for murder when he painted it, hoping the pope would pardon him.

exploreAction.targetName: Salome with the Head of John the Baptist the face on the platter
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the head on the platter — it's Caravaggio's own face. The murderer painted himself as the executed prophet, begging Rome for mercy. He died before the pardon arrived.

name: The Syndics of the Drapers' Guild
teaser: Six cloth merchants look up from their ledger as if we just walked into their meeting — a group portrait that feels like a candid moment. Rembrandt arranged them around a table covered in a Persian rug, catching each man mid-thought. It was painted in his last, bankrupt decade, and it is pure mastery of attention.

exploreAction.targetName: The Syndics of the Drapers' Guild the interruption
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the glances — each man reacts differently to our arrival, like a photo taken mid-conversation. Rembrandt's late portraits live in this moment of being seen.

name: Self-Portrait at the Age of 34
teaser: Rembrandt in a beret and fur collar, hand on hip, at the peak of his fame — confident, wealthy, almost swaggering. The gold chains and silk are real; he was Amsterdam's most sought-after painter. He would paint himself roughly ninety times across his life, and this is the portrait of the man before the fall.

exploreAction.targetName: Self-Portrait at the Age of 34 the confidence
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pose — hand on hip, chin up, a man at the top. Rembrandt would later lose his house, his money and his wife, and his self-portraits show every stage of that journey.

name: View of Delft
teaser: The city of Delft floats between water and sky, rooftops catching a silver light — the most famous cityscape of the Dutch Golden Age, and one of the rarest: Vermeer painted only about 34 works. The clouds are layered with astonishing subtlety. Proust called it 'the most beautiful painting in the world' and had a character die in front of it.

exploreAction.targetName: View of Delft the silver city
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the clouds — pink, silver, layered like nothing else in Dutch art. Proust loved this painting so much he made a character die gazing at it.

name: The Geographer
teaser: A scholar in a Japanese robe pauses over his maps, compass in hand, flooded by window light — the only Vermeer of a working man, and one of the very few of a man at all. The map behind him shows Europe and Africa; the globe is celestial. He seems to be measuring not land but knowledge itself.

exploreAction.targetName: The Geographer the paused hand
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the compass and the maps — a man caught between calculation and wonder. Vermeer painted only two scholar figures, the Geographer and the Astronomer, probably the same model.

name: The Art of Painting
teaser: An artist sits with his back to us, painting a girl crowned with laurel and holding a trumpet and a book — an allegory of the art itself, widely considered Vermeer's greatest work. The chandelier, the map, the girl's blue robe: every object is a symbol of painting's fame. Vermeer kept it unsold and unfinished in his studio until he died.

exploreAction.targetName: The Art of Painting the laurel crown
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the model — laurel wreath, trumpet, book: she's Clio, the muse of history. Vermeer painted this masterpiece and refused to sell it, keeping it in his studio for the rest of his life.

name: Lady Writing a Letter
teaser: A young woman pauses, quill in hand, looking at us with a small knowing smile — a private moment made eternal by window light. The yellow bodice, the pearl earring, the half-smile: it's the painting people compare to the Mona Lisa. The letter she writes may be a love letter; Vermeer leaves the secret with her.

exploreAction.targetName: Lady Writing a Letter the small smile
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the smile — tiny, private, directed at us. The lady has paused mid-sentence and is sharing something she'll never tell. Vermeer painted light, but he also painted secrets.

name: The Lacemaker
teaser: A girl bends over her lace pillow, fingers busy, world reduced to the geometry of threads — Vermeer's smallest painting and one of his most beloved. The bobbins blur in motion; the light is soft and warm. She never looks up, and we never want her to.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lacemaker the busy fingers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the hands — blurred with concentration, though the lace is nearly invisible to the naked eye. Vermeer painted the smallest of his works with the largest of care.

name: The Gypsy Girl
teaser: A bare-shouldered girl grins at us with a hand on her hip, painted with loose, alive brushwork — Hals captured a person in motion 300 years before photography. The smile is not posed; it's happening. The skin is painted with such quick dabs that the girl seems to breathe.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gypsy Girl the grin
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the smile — it's mid-laugh, not a portrait smile. Hals painted her in loose strokes that look spontaneous even today, a style that made him the most imitated Dutch painter.

name: Malle Babbe
teaser: A laughing woman with a pewter tankard and an owl on her shoulder — painted so loosely it looks like a snapshot from a bar fight. 'Malle' means mad; she was a real tavern regular in Haarlem. The owl was the Dutch symbol of folly, so the joke is on everyone. The brushwork is so free that 19th-century painters saw Hals as their ancestor.

exploreAction.targetName: Malle Babbe the owl
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the owl — the Dutch sign for folly, perched on a madwoman's shoulder. Hals painted her laugh so roughly it seems to have been dashed onto the canvas in seconds.

name: The Nude Maja
teaser: A woman lies naked on green pillows, arms behind her head, looking straight at us — scandalous enough that Goya was hauled before the Inquisition. In 1800s Spain, painting a nude with pubic hair was practically sedition. The identity of the model is still debated; the 'Maja' was a slang term for a feisty working-class woman. It hung in a private cabinet for years.

exploreAction.targetName: The Nude Maja the bold stare
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her eyes — she's not posing, she's looking at us with total confidence. Goya painted the clothed version too, hung facing it, and the Inquisition questioned him about both.

name: The Clothed Maja
teaser: The same woman, the same pose, but dressed in a white bodice and yellow jacket — a perfect mirror of the Nude Maja that hangs facing it in the Prado. Goya painted the pair as a dare about modesty. The clothes are painted with the same loving detail as the skin, making the joke complete.

exploreAction.targetName: The Clothed Maja the twin pose
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pose — identical to the Nude Maja, down to the hands behind the head. Goya made the pair to hang facing each other, a private wink at the Inquisition's prudery.

name: Saturn Devouring His Son
teaser: A giant with wild eyes devours a headless body, painted on the wall of Goya's own house — one of his 'Black Paintings', made in old age, deaf, sick and disgusted with the world. The myth says Saturn ate his children to stop them overthrowing him. Goya's Saturn is not a god but a mad animal. He never intended it for public display.

exploreAction.targetName: Saturn Devouring His Son the wild eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eyes — terrified and ravenous at once. Goya painted this on his dining-room wall in his deaf, bitter old age, and it was only discovered after his death.

name: Witches' Sabbath
teaser: A great goat in a robe presides over a circle of witches while bats crowd the sky — Goya's savage satire of superstition and the Inquisition that fed it. The goat is the Devil, and the worshippers are old, ugly and starving, not glamorous. Goya painted it for the Duchess of Alba's country house, as part of a room of witchcraft themes.

exploreAction.targetName: Witches' Sabbath the great goat
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the goat — robed like a priest, presiding over a congregation of fools. Goya's witchcraft scenes were his protest against superstition, painted for a duchess's country retreat.

name: The Intervention of the Sabine Women
teaser: Roman women throw themselves between their fathers and their husbands, babies in arms, halting a battle — painted while David was in prison, and shown to win his freedom. The composition is a frieze of arms and bodies, the women at the exact center of the clash. David meant it as a call for peace after the Terror of the French Revolution.

exploreAction.targetName: The Intervention of the Sabine Women the peacemakers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the center — women with infants stepping between two armies. David painted it in prison and displayed it to argue for reconciliation after the Revolution's bloodiest years.

name: The Charging Chasseur
teaser: An officer on a rearing horse turns to look back at us, saber drawn, while smoke rises — painted when Géricault was only 21, and it made him famous overnight. The horse's eye rolls in panic; the officer is already doomed. It was meant to flatter Napoleon's army, but the tension in it suggests the coming disaster.

exploreAction.targetName: The Charging Chasseur the rear
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the horse's eye — that's fear, not glory. Géricault painted the rearing cavalryman at 21 and caught something the official war painters missed: the panic inside the pose.

name: The Slave Ship
teaser: A burning ship disappears into a storm of red and gold while the sea boils with drowning figures — a painting that is also an indictment. Turner based it on the Zong massacre, when slavers threw 132 enslaved people overboard for insurance money. The beauty and the horror share one canvas. Ruskin, who owned it, called it the most sublime picture in existence.

exploreAction.targetName: The Slave Ship the red sea
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water — look closely, and the beautiful waves are chained hands and faces. Turner painted the horror of the slave trade inside a sunset so gorgeous it hurts.

name: The Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons
teaser: London's parliament burns in a hurricane of orange flame reflected in the Thames — Turner watched the fire from a boat and painted it from direct observation, sketches first. The Houses of Parliament were destroyed in October 1834. Turner's fire paintings turned a disaster into a vision of apocalypse, and he sold them as souvenirs of the event.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burning of the Houses the orange river
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Thames — it's on fire too, the reflection doubling the blaze. Turner went out in a boat to watch the real fire and painted the spectacle as a kind of sacred disaster.

name: Dedham Vale
teaser: A quiet valley in Suffolk with a winding river, cows and a distant church — the landscape Constable grew up in and painted his whole life. The church tower is Dedham's St Mary's; the sunburst breaks through after rain. Constable said painting was 'another word for feeling', and this view is his feeling for home.

exploreAction.targetName: Dedham Vale the home valley
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky — rain clearing to sun, the moment Constable loved best. He painted his home valley over and over, calling the sensation of it 'the sound of water escaping from mill dams'.

name: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows
teaser: The cathedral spire rises over a flooded meadow while a rainbow arcs across the storm — Constable's most personal landscape, painted in grief after his wife died. The rainbow spans the whole canvas, a promise after the storm. It took him two years and multiple versions; he considered it his greatest work.

exploreAction.targetName: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows the rainbow
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the rainbow — it crosses the entire painting, arching over the cathedral. Constable painted it while mourning his wife, and the storm-to-rainbow is his grief finding hope.

name: The Meeting (Bonjour, Monsieur Courbet)
teaser: A rich collector greets the artist on a country road while his servant kneels — Courbet painted himself as the equal of the aristocrat, a walking manifesto. The collector Alfred Bruyas bows; Courbet, with his painting kit, stands tall. The sky is huge, the road long. It's the Realist credo in paint: the artist is no one's servant.

exploreAction.targetName: The Meeting the bowing collector
exploreAction.instruction: Look at who bows — the rich man tips his hat, the artist returns the greeting as an equal. Courbet painted himself as the sun of his own universe, and his patron as a respectful planet.

name: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe
teaser: A naked woman picnics with two fully dressed men while another woman bathes in the stream — the painting that scandalized Paris and ignited modern art. The nude stares straight at us, unashamed; the men talk on, ignoring her. Manet borrowed the composition from an old engraving of a classical scene, but set it in his own time — the insult was the setting, not the nudity.

exploreAction.targetName: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe the unashamed stare
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman's gaze — direct, unembarrassed, aimed at us. Napoleon III's salon rejected it, so Manet showed it in the Salon des Refusés and changed art forever.

name: At the Races
teaser: Horses and jockeys bunch at the starting line while a carriage waits — Degas's love of speed and bodies in motion, painted in soft country light. He sketched at the track for years, obsessed with the horse's stride. The jockeys' silks blaze against the pale green. It's a painting of anticipation, the moment before the gallop.

exploreAction.targetName: At the Races the starting line
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the horses — muscles bunched, ears forward, one pawing. Degas studied horse racing like a scientist and painted the instant before the race, not the race itself.

name: A Woman Ironing
teaser: A laundress leans her whole body into the iron, face hidden, work consuming her — Degas's unsentimental portrait of labor. She's not pretty, not posed; she's tired, and the iron is heavy. Degas painted the laundresses and dancers of Paris with the same honest eye. The white cloth and her white cap make the canvas almost abstract.

exploreAction.targetName: A Woman Ironing the heavy iron
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her posture — the whole body presses down on the iron. Degas painted working women without romance: she's not a symbol, she's someone who irons all day.

name: In the Loge
teaser: A woman in a black dress watches the opera through opera glasses while a man across the way stares at her instead of the stage — a sharp social comment from the only American in the Impressionist circle. She holds the glasses to the performance; he holds his to her. Cassatt painted the watcher being watched.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Loge the watcher watched
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the man in the background — his glasses point at her, not the stage. Cassatt flipped the male gaze of her era into a painting about who really watches whom.

name: The Water Lily Pond
teaser: A green arched bridge crosses a pond of water lilies, the light dappled to near-dissolution — the garden at Giverny that Monet built, dug and flooded for the sole purpose of painting it. He painted this view dozens of times as the light changed. The Japanese bridge was his own design, inspired by woodblock prints he collected.

exploreAction.targetName: The Water Lily Pond the green bridge
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water — the lilies, the sky and the bridge all dissolve into patches of light. Monet created the garden, then painted the garden, then the garden became the painting.

name: San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk
teaser: The Venetian church floats on a mirror of violet water at twilight, so dissolved in color it nearly disappears — painted on Monet's only visit to Venice, at 68. He worked from his gondola, chasing the light as it died. The painting is almost abstract: church, water and sky melt into one substance. He returned to Venice's views again and again in the studio.

exploreAction.targetName: San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk the violet mirror
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how the church melts into the water — Venice reduced to pure color and light. Monet visited Venice once, at 68, and painted its twilight until the light gave out.

name: Two Sisters (On the Terrace)
teaser: Two girls on a terrace at Chatou, one holding a small ball, the river glittering behind them — Renoir's idea of happiness: sunshine, youth and a view. The older sister was a model who posed for several Renoir works; the younger one was a real friend. The brushwork is loose, the palette warm. It's the painting that made collectors fight for it.

exploreAction.targetName: Two Sisters (On the Terrace) the terrace
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light on the girls' faces — soft, warm, mid-summer. Renoir painted joy, and this terrace above the Seine at Chatou was his favorite place to find it.

name: Girl with a Watering Can
teaser: A little girl in a blue dress stands in a garden with a red watering can, painted with the freshness of a snapshot — Renoir's niece or a neighbor's child, identity still debated. The can is the red anchor of the whole canvas. Renoir said he painted children with 'the same delight as flowers'. It is pure, radiant summertime.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl with a Watering Can the red can
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the red watering can — the one loud note in a garden of greens and blues. Renoir painted children as happily as flowers, and this girl is summer itself.

name: Parade de Cirque
teaser: A circus sideshow glows under gaslight, the ringmaster and musicians caught in Seurat's pointillist dots — a night scene built of tiny separate touches of color. The light is artificial, ghostly, falling on pale faces. Seurat used the new science of color to paint the old magic of the circus. It's one of his few night paintings.

exploreAction.targetName: Parade de Cirque the gaslight
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the glow — artificial, greenish, unlike daylight. Seurat built the whole scene from tiny dots of color and made gaslight itself the subject.

name: Jas de Bouffan
teaser: The family farmhouse among tall trees, painted in blocky planes of color — Cézanne's apprenticeship in turning nature into geometry. He grew up at Jas de Bouffan and painted it dozens of times. The trunks are columns, the foliage is architecture. This is where he worked out the system that made him 'the father of us all' — Picasso's words.

exploreAction.targetName: Jas de Bouffan the blocky trees
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the trees — they're not painted, they're built, trunk by trunk, plane by plane. Cézanne spent his youth here working out how to make landscape into structure, and modern art followed.

name: Tahitian Women on the Beach
teaser: Two Tahitian women sit by the shore, one in a red pareo, one in white, their gazes calm and far away — painted in the first months of Gauguin's escape to the South Seas. He had left Paris, his job and his family to find 'primitive' paradise. The colors are flat, the forms monumental. The paradise was real to him, at least for a while.

exploreAction.targetName: Tahitian Women on the Beach the calm gazes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the stillness — two women, the sea, no hurry. Gauguin fled Europe for this, painting with flat colors and simple shapes that would change art forever.

name: The Toilette
teaser: A woman at her dressing table, back to us, reflected dimly in the mirror — an intimate glimpse of private life by the painter of Paris's nightlife. Lautrec's view is tender and respectful, not leering. The pastel colors glow like gaslight. For a man who lived in brothels and bars, this quiet scene is the other side of his world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Toilette the dim mirror
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mirror — you can barely see her reflection, an invitation to imagine. Lautrec, chronicler of the Moulin Rouge, painted this private scene with remarkable gentleness.

name: The Tree of Life
teaser: A golden tree with spiral branches stretches across a wall of mosaic — part of Klimt's masterpiece frieze for the Palais Stoclet in Brussels. The tree holds the universe: an embracing couple, a waiting woman, birds of paradise. The spirals are life itself, curling endlessly. It's Art Nouveau's greatest monument, still in the house it was made for.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tree of Life the golden spirals
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the branches — every one curls into a spiral, growth without end. Klimt designed it as a mosaic wall for a Brussels palace, and the tree still holds its place there today.

name: Cossacks
teaser: Cossack riders sweep through a landscape of pure color and line — Kandinsky's leap from scenery into music made visible. The riders are still there, but barely: the painting is about speed, sound and color crashing together. He titled it Cossacks, but the real subject is 'the sense of battle' as pure form. It marks the exact moment abstract art began.

exploreAction.targetName: Cossacks the riders in color
exploreAction.instruction: Look for the riders — two curved lines and a lance in a storm of color. Kandinsky was moving from painting scenes to painting sounds, and this canvas is the border crossing.

name: Blue Nude
teaser: A woman arches in blue against a tropical backdrop, one arm over her head, one leg lifted — Matisse's response to Picasso's Les Demoiselles, and his own leap into bold distortion. The body is simplified, almost carved. Critics mocked it as ugly; Matisse said he painted 'the essential character' of the figure. It shocked Paris and freed painting from copying nature.

exploreAction.targetName: Blue Nude the blue arch
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pose — no photograph could catch it; it's invented, expressive, pure sculpture in paint. Matisse made the body blue on purpose, to prove color carries emotion alone.

name: Soft Construction with Boiled Beans (Premonition of Civil War)
teaser: A giant body tears itself apart on a barren plain, one limb strangling its own torso — painted six months before the Spanish Civil War actually started, and Dalí called it his prophecy. The 'boiled beans' of the title are the poverty of the landscape. The creature is war itself, self-destroying. Dalí insisted the painting 'prophesied' the war; skeptics note he dated it cleverly.

exploreAction.targetName: Soft Construction the tearing body
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the body — it's tearing itself apart, a war machine with no enemy but itself. Dalí painted this premonition of civil war in 1936, months before Spain actually erupted.

name: Ram's Head White Hollyhock and Little Hills
teaser: A bleached ram's skull floats above a rolling desert landscape, a perfect circle of bone over the earth's curves — O'Keeffe's most famous New Mexico image. She collected the skull on a walk and paired it with hills and a flower. The painting is about time: the skull that outlasts the flesh, the hills that outlast the skull.

exploreAction.targetName: Ram's Head White Hollyhock the floating skull
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the skull — it hovers over the hills like a moon. O'Keeffe found it in the New Mexico desert and turned death's head into a meditation on time.

name: Eight Elvises
teaser: Eight identical Elvis Presleys in cowboy gear, drawn as a repeating row of silver gunslingers — Warhol's largest Elvis and his first to repeat the same image eight times. The silver paint makes it a room-length mirror. It sold in 2008 for over $100 million, among the most expensive paintings ever. Elvis, like Marilyn and the soup can, was an image to be multiplied.

exploreAction.targetName: Eight Elvises the silver cowboys
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the repetition — eight cowboys in a row, a movie still turned into wallpaper. Warhol printed Elvis eight times and sold the result for over a hundred million dollars.

name: Shot Marilyns
teaser: Four panels of Marilyn Monroe's face in screaming color, each pair of the same image — named for the day a performance artist shot a bullet through a stack of them. The five canvases were leaning against each other when Dorothy Podber fired a pistol through them, and the four surviving works took their name from the bullet holes. They are among the most valuable paintings in the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Shot Marilyns the bullet holes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Marilyn faces — identical except for color. A performance artist shot a bullet through the stack, and the survivors became 'Shot Marilyns', worth nine figures.

name: Girl with Ball
teaser: A girl juggles a ball above her head in Ben-Day dots and bold black outlines, speech-bubble style — Lichtenstein lifting comic-book art onto the gallery wall. The composition mimics a single frame, complete with printed dots. Critics argued about whether it was art; Lichtenstein argued that a painting of a ball 'is a ball'.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl with Ball the ben-day dots
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the dots — printed texture painted by hand, the comic strip made monumental. Lichtenstein turned a comic-book frame into a museum piece and started a war of opinions.

name: Lavender Mist (Number 1, 1950)
teaser: An all-over web of poured paint in lavender, grey and black, built by dripping from above — Pollock's 'action painting', where the canvas lay on the floor and the artist walked around it. He called it 'energy and motion made visible'. The lavender comes from a mix of white, black and alizarin that reads as a soft haze. He worked on it for months, cutting it to size.

exploreAction.targetName: Lavender Mist the poured web
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the layers — paint poured, dripped and flung, some lines under others. Pollock worked on the floor, and the painting records the choreography of his whole body.

name: No. 14
teaser: Two soft rectangles of red and maroon float on a field of the same color, edges bleeding into one another — a Rothko built for staring, not for reading. The rectangles are not shapes but moods; he wanted viewers to stand close and be absorbed. He said he painted 'basic human emotions — tragedy, ecstasy, doom'. The edges glow because he layered thinned paint over warm grounds.

exploreAction.targetName: No. 14 the glowing rectangles
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the edges of the rectangles — they vibrate, as if the color itself is breathing. Rothko wanted you close enough to feel the painting, not to understand it.

name: Three Studies of Lucian Freud
teaser: The painter Lucian Freud twisted into three cages of brushstroke and color, each panel a different distortion of the same face — Bacon's portrait of his rival and friend. The figures sit in bare rooms, mouths open, bodies smeared. Bacon destroyed most of his portraits; these three survived because Freud prized them. They sold for $142 million in 2013.

exploreAction.targetName: Three Studies of Lucian Freud the three cages
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faces — the same man three ways, each more unsettled than the last. Bacon painted his friend and rival Lucian Freud in panels that sold for $142 million.

name: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy
teaser: A fashion designer and his wife sit in their sunlit flat, the white cat Percy on the husband's knee — a double portrait that became the face of 1970s Britain. The Clerks were friends, not lovers; their marriage was one of friendship. The light pours through the glass table and the white walls. Hockney's eye for domestic calm made it one of the most beloved British paintings of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy the white cat
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the cat — his name is Percy, and he's the third subject of the portrait. Hockney painted his friends in a flat full of light, and Britain adopted it as its own.

name: Detroit Industry
