teaser: A whole factory civilization covers the walls of the Detroit Institute of Arts — 27 fresco panels of workers, machines, science and industry, painted in 1933. Rivera spent months in the factories drawing workers and machines, then built scaffolds to paint the walls directly. The panels show everything from birth to the assembly line. It is considered the greatest mural cycle in America.

exploreAction.targetName: Detroit Industry the factory walls
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the scale — 27 panels wrapping an entire court, every inch a working factory or a worker's body. Rivera spent months inside Detroit's plants before painting its portrait on the walls.

name: Tableau I
teaser: Black grid lines and blocks of red, yellow and blue on white — Mondrian's search for the absolute, reduced to its minimum grammar. He banned curves, diagonals and finally even green. The balance is so delicate that moving one line by a millimeter would collapse it. He called his style 'neoplasticism': pure plastic expression through pure form.

exploreAction.targetName: Tableau I the perfect grid
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the grid — not a single line is decorative; every one is load-bearing. Mondrian spent thirty years removing things from painting until only this balance remained.

name: Moses
teaser: A bearded giant sits with the tablets of law, muscles tense, eyes blazing — carved by Michelangelo for the tomb of Pope Julius II, a project that consumed him for 40 years. Legend says the artist struck the knee and shouted 'Speak!' at the sculpture. The horns on Moses' head follow the Latin Vulgate's translation of 'rays of light'. It sits in San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome.

exploreAction.targetName: Moses the blazing eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eyes — they see something we can't. Michelangelo carved the horns from a Bible translation, and legend says he was so moved he commanded the statue to speak.

name: Doni Tondo
teaser: The Holy Family in a circle, with naked youths lounging behind them — the only panel painting Michelangelo ever finished, made for a Florentine wedding. The round format was a wedding tradition. The background nudes are probably a classical contrast to the sacred scene. The frame is the original one, carved with the family's symbols.

exploreAction.targetName: Doni Tondo the circle
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the ring of bodies behind the family — athletes from the pagan world watching the Christian story. Michelangelo's only completed panel painting, made for a wedding, in its original carved frame.

name: Salvator Mundi
teaser: Christ holds a crystal globe in one hand and raises the other in blessing — a painting with a rock-star history: lost for centuries, rediscovered, and sold in 2017 for $450 million, the highest price ever paid for a work of art. Whether every brushstroke is Leonardo's is debated, but the sfumato haze over the face is his signature. It has not been publicly shown since the sale.

exploreAction.targetName: Salvator Mundi the crystal globe
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the globe — a transparent sphere painted with almost photographic clarity, the surface suggesting both glass and a world. Lost, found, and sold for $450 million: the most expensive painting ever.

name: The School of Athens
teaser: Plato and Aristotle walk through a vast hall of philosophers, mathematicians and artists — the perfect image of classical thought, painted on the Vatican's wall. Raphael put Leonardo's face on Plato and his own portrait at the right edge. Euclid bends over a slate, Pythagoras writes, Diogenes sprawls on the steps. It is the Renaissance's self-portrait of the mind.

exploreAction.targetName: The School of Athens the philosophers
exploreAction.instruction: Look for two men at center — Plato points to heaven, Aristotle to the earth. That's the whole history of philosophy in one gesture, painted by a 26-year-old.

name: The Haywain Triptych
teaser: The whole human comedy rides a giant haycart toward hell: angels, popes, lovers and fools all grabbing at the hay — Bosch's satire of greed, painted as a triptych that opens like a book. The left panel shows the fall of Adam, the right shows hell. Everyone, from peasants to popes, fights for the same worthless hay. Bosch's hell is full of invented monsters.

exploreAction.targetName: The Haywain Triptych the haycart
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the cart — everyone from the pope down is climbing on for a share of hay. Bosch painted greed as a pilgrimage to hell, and his hell is stuffed with creatures no one had imagined before.

name: The Seven Deadly Sins
teaser: Four circular scenes around a central eye-of-God, each ring showing one of the seven sins in miniature — a tabletop painting meant to warn its owner. In the center, Christ rises from the tomb inside the pupil of God's eye. Each sin gets its own busy little world: gluttony at a table, pride before a mirror. It is Bosch's most complete moral map.

exploreAction.targetName: The Seven Deadly Sins the eye of god
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the center — Christ inside the pupil of God's eye, watching every sin in the rings around him. Bosch painted the warning on a tabletop so the owner saw it at every meal.

name: The Hunters in the Snow
teaser: Hunters trudge home through snow while villagers skate on a frozen pond below — the most famous winter scene in Western art, one of a series of the months. The dogs are tired, the hunters empty-handed, but the valley glows with cold light. Bruegel painted winter as both hardship and beauty. The painting has inspired films, poems and centuries of Christmas cards.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hunters in the Snow the cold valley
exploreAction.instruction: Look down the hill — a whole village is alive in the ice, skating and playing while the hunters return empty-handed. Bruegel saw beauty and work in the same frozen frame.

name: The Fall of Icarus
teaser: A ploughman, a shepherd and a fisherman all ignore the splash in the sea where Icarus falls — the myth told by its absence. Only a pair of legs is visible, kicking in the water; the sun still shines, the ship sails on. Bruegel's point is devastating: the world does not stop for tragedy. The poem 'Musée des Beaux-Arts' by Auden made it famous.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fall of Icarus the splash
exploreAction.instruction: Look into the water — just two legs and a splash at the bottom right. The farmer, the shepherd and the sailor all carry on: the world's indifference, painted in 1560.

name: The Elevation of the Cross
teaser: Muscles strain as a dozen men haul Christ's cross upright, the diagonal of the beam cutting through the sky — Rubens's breakthrough work, painted at 33 for Antwerp's cathedral. The bodies are Baroque drama made flesh: every tendon, every grimace. The painting had been damaged and repainted over centuries; a recent restoration revealed Rubens's original, more vivid colors.

exploreAction.targetName: The Elevation of the Cross the straining muscles
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the diagonal — the cross cuts across the whole canvas, every body straining against it. Rubens painted this at 33 and became the most famous painter in Europe overnight.

name: The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus
teaser: Twin brothers carry off twin sisters on horseback, a tangle of limbs, silk and horseflesh — Rubens's hymn to the human body in motion. The scene is from Greek myth: Castor and Pollux abduct Phoebe and Hilaeira. The composition spirals around the horses like a fountain. Rubens made the impossible look effortless, and the canvas glows with flesh tones.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus the tangle
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the spiral — two horses, four riders, all turning around a single center. Rubens choreographed flesh and horse into a wheel of motion that has never been equaled.

name: Et in Arcadia ego
teaser: Shepherds in a golden landscape read the words on a tomb: 'I too am in Arcadia' — even paradise contains death. The inscription is the painting's whole argument, and scholars still debate who speaks it: Death, or the dead shepherd. The shepherds' postures spell the letters of the phrase. The calm is the terror.

exploreAction.targetName: Et in Arcadia ego the tomb
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the tomb — 'Even in Arcadia, I exist': death speaking inside paradise. Poussin arranged the shepherds' gestures to echo the letters of the Latin inscription.

name: The Rape of the Sabine Women
teaser: Romans seize Sabine women in a whirlwind of columns, shields and outstretched arms — the myth of Rome's founding, painted with archaeological precision. Poussin studied ancient sculpture and rebuilt Rome's early chaos. The architecture is exact; the violence is choreographed. It is a history painting that makes history feel like an opera.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rape of the Sabine Women the whirlwind
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the architecture — every column is archaeologically exact, the city rebuilt in paint. Poussin staged Rome's founding myth like a director, and his stage still stands.

name: The Triumph of Neptune and Amphitrite
teaser: Neptune drives a chariot of seahorses through a frothing sea, sea gods and nymphs swirling around — a ceiling of ocean for Cardinal Richelieu. The composition whirls like a wave. Poussin painted the classical gods as perfectly ordered energy: wild but controlled. The painting's cool blues and golds were made for a palace interior.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of Neptune the seahorses
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the horses — they're half fish, half horse, carving through the sea like the waves themselves. Poussin painted this for Cardinal Richelieu, a ceiling of myth for a palace.

name: The Stolen Kiss
teaser: A young woman slips away from her chaperones into a doorway for a quick kiss — a Rococo fantasy of love stolen in passing. Fragonard painted the 'love series' of four panels for Madame du Barry. The light, the silks, the barely-contained grin: it is flirtation as high art. The painting's lightness hides a sharp eye for real emotion.

exploreAction.targetName: The Stolen Kiss the doorway
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the doorway — the kiss happens in a half-open space, one step from discovery. Fragonard painted a series of love's stages for Madame du Barry's pavilion.

name: The Love Letter
teaser: A woman presses a letter to her heart, another note tucked in her corsage, surrounded by roses — a painting of a secret, half-told. The letter is from a lover, obviously; the roses are for him, probably. Fragonard's brushwork is all speed and shimmer. The canvas is small, intimate, meant to be read close.

exploreAction.targetName: The Love Letter the pressed note
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her hand — the letter pressed to her chest like it's part of her. Fragonard painted secrets in silk and rose, and this one stays untold.

name: Diana Leaving Her Bath
teaser: The goddess Diana sits at a pool's edge with a nymph, her hunt complete, her skin pearlescent — Boucher's favorite subject, painted for Madame de Pompadour. The pearls, the doves, the blue silk: it is luxury as mythology. Boucher was the king's first painter and the Rococo's most successful artist. Diana was also the name of his patron's daughter.

exploreAction.targetName: Diana Leaving Her Bath the pearls
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pearls and the porcelain skin — a goddess rendered as the height of French fashion. Boucher painted Diana for the king's favorite, and the myth is really about luxury.

name: Madame de Pompadour
teaser: The king's favorite stands in a garden with a book, a fan and a dog, dressed in green silk — the portrait of the most powerful woman in France who was not the queen. Boucher painted her many times; this one is the official image of her learning and taste. The book is open, the library is behind her: Pompadour was a patron of the Encyclopédie.

exploreAction.targetName: Madame de Pompadour the green silk
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the book in her hand — the king's mistress was one of the most educated women in France, and she paid for the Encyclopédie. Boucher's portrait is a job application to history.

name: The Fête Champêtre
teaser: Elegant couples picnic in a park while a statue watches over them — the 'fête galante', a genre Watteau invented. His people are always just about to leave, or just arrived, the mood bittersweet. The silks shimmer, the trees are theatrical. Watteau died at 36, leaving a genre of melancholy pleasure that defined French painting for a generation.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fête Champêtre the park picnic
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mood — everyone is elegant and no one is happy. Watteau invented the 'fête galante' and filled it with the ache of pleasures that end.

name: Gilles
teaser: A white clown stands alone in full costume, arms at his sides, looking straight at us with an expression between vacancy and sorrow — one of the strangest and most haunting paintings in French art. Gilles is the stock comic servant of the commedia dell'arte, but nothing here is comic. The four figures at his feet chatter on, ignoring him. It is the loneliest portrait of a performer ever painted.

exploreAction.targetName: Gilles the white clown
exploreAction.instruction: Look at his face — blank, patient, heartbreaking. The comedians at his feet talk among themselves; the clown performs his solitude for us alone.

name: Grande Odalisque
teaser: A woman reclines on blue silk with her back to us, her spine impossibly long — Ingres elongated her back by three vertebrae for elegance, and critics howled. 'She has no bones,' they said. Ingres replied that beauty mattered more than anatomy. The turban, the fan, the pipe: an oriental fantasy of the harem, painted for Napoleon's sister.

exploreAction.targetName: Grande Odalisque the long back
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the back — count the vertebrae; there are too many. Ingres added three extra bones to make the line more beautiful, and art criticism has argued about it ever since.

name: Napoleon on His Imperial Throne
teaser: Napoleon sits on a gilded throne like a Byzantine icon, hand on scepter, halo-like crown behind him — the most regal image of the emperor ever painted. Ingres borrowed the pose from ancient Roman emperors and medieval icons. The eagle rug, the ermine, the gold: total power as total ornament. It was exhibited in 1806, the year after Austerlitz.

exploreAction.targetName: Napoleon on His Imperial Throne the throne
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pose — frontal, frozen, like a Byzantine Christ. Ingres painted Napoleon as a living icon of power, and the emperor reportedly loved it.

name: The Source
teaser: A girl pours water from a jar in a perfect classical pose, the stream falling in a single silver line — Ingres's ideal of beauty, begun when he was 36 and finished 30 years later. The pose quotes the ancient Greek sculpture of Aphrodite. It became the most reproduced nude in history, adorning everything from textbooks to soap ads. Ingres called it the 'living tradition'.

exploreAction.targetName: The Source the silver stream
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water — a single unbroken line from jar to pool. Ingres worked on this canvas for 30 years, and it became the most copied nude painting in the world.

name: The Gleaners
teaser: Three women bend to gather leftover grain in a vast field, the harvest already stacked behind them — a painting of labor made monumental. Before Millet, peasants in art were background figures; here they fill the frame. The gleaners were the poorest of the poor, legally allowed only the fallen grain. Millet painted their dignity, and the rich called it dangerous. It hangs in the Louvre.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gleaners the bending women
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the scale — the women are huge, the harvest stacks are tiny behind them. Millet made the poorest workers the heroes of a painting, and the wealthy called it subversive.

name: The Angelus
teaser: A farmer and his wife pause in the twilight, heads bowed, potato fork and basket set down, as the church bell rings the evening prayer — the most reproduced religious image of the 19th century. The couple may actually be praying over a grave; X-rays showed a small coffin under the basket. Millet painted memory, poverty and faith in one humble scene.

exploreAction.targetName: The Angelus the bowed heads
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two figures — tools set down, heads bowed, the bell ringing from the distant spire. X-rays later revealed a small coffin hidden under the basket: they may be praying at a grave.

name: The Grieving Parents
teaser: A father and mother kneel in stone at the edge of a war cemetery, their bodies folded into grief itself — Kollwitz's monument to her own son, killed in 1914. She worked on the figures for over a decade, simplifying them into near-abstraction. The parents kneel at the grave of her son Peter in Belgium. The monument is considered the greatest war memorial of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: The Grieving Parents the kneeling grief
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the postures — the father's clenched back, the mother's folded arms. Kollwitz carved her own grief into stone for the son she lost, and it took her fourteen years.

name: Portrait of Madame X
teaser: A society beauty in a black gown with jeweled straps poses with unsettling confidence — the scandal of the 1884 Paris Salon. The strap was originally painted slipping off her shoulder, which shocked Paris so much Sargent repainted it. The portrait ruined his reputation in France and he moved to London. It later became one of the Met's most beloved paintings.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of Madame X the black gown
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the straps — one was originally falling off the shoulder, and the scandal was so loud Sargent repainted it and left Paris. The woman is Virginie Amélie Gautreau, a famous beauty.

name: The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit
teaser: Four sisters scatter through a Paris apartment — one in a doorway, one on a rug, two in the middle — arranged like a mysterious composition of presence and absence. The giant blue vases are real Japanese ceramics in the Boit family. The girls never look at us or at each other. The empty space in the center is the fifth figure of the painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Daughters of Edward Darley Boit the vases
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the center — nothing there but rug and wall, the space itself as a presence. The girls scatter through the rooms, each alone, and the vases were the family's real ceramics.

name: Nocturne in Black and Gold — The Falling Rocket
teaser: A fireworks burst over Cremorne Gardens dissolves into black and gold mist — the painting that made Whistler a public enemy of the critic Ruskin. Ruskin accused him of 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face', and Whistler sued for libel. He won the case and was awarded one farthing. The painting is now worth about a million times that.

exploreAction.targetName: Nocturne in Black and Gold the rocket
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the explosion — sparks dissolving into dark mist, almost abstract in 1875. Whistler's 'nocturnes' sparked a libel trial when Ruskin called them a pot of paint flung at the public.

name: The Gulf Stream
teaser: A lone sailor lies on the deck of a broken boat surrounded by sharks, a waterspout on the horizon — nature's indifference, painted by America's greatest watercolorist in oil. The boat has no mast and no sail; the sharks circle. Homer painted it after years in the Caribbean and the Bahamas. He showed it unfinished for years, letting the world worry about the sailor's fate.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gulf Stream the circling sharks
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sharks — patient, circling, already sure. Homer painted a man alone with the sea, and the sea does not care. He kept the sailor's fate unresolved on purpose.

name: Freedom from Want
teaser: A family gathers around a Thanksgiving turkey while a grandmother carries it in like a queen — the most famous of Rockwell's Four Freedoms, painted from the president's 1941 speech. The scene is his own family's tradition. The painting ran in the Saturday Evening Post and became a national symbol during World War II. Rockwell's models were real neighbors and relatives, including his cook's daughter.

exploreAction.targetName: Freedom from Want the turkey
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faces — every one of them is a real person Rockwell knew, and the turkey is his own family's. The painting helped sell war bonds; it was an image of the home worth fighting for.

name: Boy and Dog in a Johnnypump
teaser: A boy and his dog under a bright red sun, painted in raw, confident strokes with words scattered around — Basquiat at 21, already painting like a voice that had to be heard. The 'johnnypump' is a fire hydrant; the scene is a kid's summer memory. The painting is full of his signature motifs: the crown, the sun, the bones. It sold for over $100 million in 2020.

exploreAction.targetName: Boy and Dog in a Johnnypump the red sun
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the red sun — a kid's drawing made monumental. Basquiat painted this at 21 from memory of summertime, and it sold for over $100 million.

name: Hollywood Africans
teaser: Three Black artists — Basquiat, his friend Toxic and the rapper Rammellzee — face us in a triptych of spray-painted words and crowns, a portrait of friendship and ambition. The words list the stereotypes Hollywood assigned them. The crowns mark them as kings. It is Basquiat's manifesto: we are the stars, and we know what you call us.

exploreAction.targetName: Hollywood Africans the crowns
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the words — the slurs and stereotypes Hollywood used, scrawled as graffiti over the artists' portraits. Basquiat crowned himself and his friends against them.

name: Rabbit
teaser: A stainless-steel inflatable rabbit, polished to a mirror — Koons's most famous sculpture, and one of the most expensive ever sold: $91 million in 2019. It's a balloon animal made permanent, weightless-looking and heavier than it looks. Koons had the surface polished to invisibility, so the sculpture reflects the viewer completely. Critics have argued about it for decades; the price settled little.

exploreAction.targetName: Rabbit the mirror surface
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the surface — it reflects the whole room, polished steel disguised as plastic. Koons's Rabbit sold for $91 million, making a balloon animal the third most expensive sculpture ever.

name: Ascending and Descending
teaser: Monks climb a staircase that goes forever up while others descend forever down — on the same stairs, on the same side. Escher's impossible geometry plays a trick called the Penrose stairs. The monks on top of the building are walking in circles within a circle. Escher said he was just showing what is impossible in the world and possible in art.

exploreAction.targetName: Ascending and Descending the endless stairs
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the staircase — follow any monk and he returns to where he started, always climbing. Escher built the Penrose impossible stairs, and monks march them forever.

name: Drawing Hands
teaser: Two hands draw each other into existence, each pencil feeding the other — the perfect image of self-creation, and Escher's most popular work. The paper curls as if the drawn hands are lifting off the page. Escher said he enjoyed the 'surprise of the moment when the drawn hands come to life'. It is a paradox you can't stop looking at.

exploreAction.targetName: Drawing Hands the self-drawing
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the paper — it's curling, the drawn hand is coming off the page to draw the hand that draws it. Escher made the paradox of creation visible in a single image.

name: Waterfall
teaser: A waterfall pours from the top of a tower and flows downhill — only to fall again from the same point, a perpetual-motion machine. The trick is the Penrose triangle, repeated so the water always descends and always returns to the top. The terraces are built in impossible geometry. Escher delighted in drawing machines that defy physics.

exploreAction.targetName: Waterfall the endless fall
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water — it falls from the tower, flows down, and arrives back at the top of the same tower. Escher built a perpetual-motion machine out of the impossible triangle.

name: Day and Night
teaser: White birds fly from a dark town into a bright one while black birds fly the other way, the two halves interlocking like a puzzle — Escher's most famous print. The fields tessellate into birds as the eye travels upward. The town is inspired by the Dutch landscape he knew. It is the clearest demonstration of his belief that pattern and illusion are the same thing.

exploreAction.targetName: Day and Night the interlocking birds
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky — the fields turn into birds, white over dark, black over light, perfectly interlocking. Escher made the landscape tessellate into flight.

name: The Abbey in the Oakwood
teaser: A ruined abbey stands in a snowbound grove of bare oaks, a funeral procession threading toward the gate — death painted as a landscape, in grey and silver. Friedrich made the ruins a memento mori: the abbey was once alive, the trees are bare, the mourners enter the gate. The moon is a pale coin. It was painted the year his friend died.

exploreAction.targetName: The Abbey in the Oakwood the ruined gate
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the gate — mourners carry a coffin into a ruin older than memory. Friedrich painted his friend's death as a landscape of ice, oaks and a pale moon.

name: Moonrise over the Sea
teaser: Three people sit on a rock watching the moon rise over the sea, the light a path across the water — the Romantic image of longing, painted over and over by Friedrich. The figures look away from us, toward the light. The painting is small, quiet, and enormous in feeling. It is the visual definition of Sehnsucht, the ache for the far and unreachable.

exploreAction.targetName: Moonrise over the Sea the watchers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the three figures — they've turned their backs on us to watch the moon. Friedrich painted longing itself: the ache for the light on the water.

name: Flood at Port-Marly
teaser: The Seine has flooded the village of Port-Marly, houses reflected in the standing water, sky and flood merging — Sisley's finest flood painting, one of a series. The village flooded for real, and Sisley painted it from a boat. The reflections are so exact the water looks like a second sky. He painted the same village flooding again in 1876, obsessed with the light on the flood.

exploreAction.targetName: Flood at Port-Marly the reflected village
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the water — the houses and sky double themselves perfectly. Sisley painted the real flood of Port-Marly from a rowboat, obsessed with the mirror the water made.

name: The Bridge at Moret-sur-Loing
teaser: A stone bridge arches over the river Loing in autumn light, the water striped with reflections — the view Sisley painted over and over in the last years of his life. The bridge had a mill and a church behind it; he painted the scene at every hour and season. The canvas glows with a soft, patient light. Sisley died poor and unknown; today the bridge is named for him.

exploreAction.targetName: The Bridge at Moret-sur-Loing the arch
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the reflection — the bridge's arch doubles in the water, exact and still. Sisley painted this bridge obsessively in his final years; today the town named it after him.

name: Boulevard Montmartre at Night
teaser: The great Paris boulevard dissolves into gaslight and shadow, carriages and streetlamps caught in wet-night light — Pissarro's city at its most atmospheric. He painted a whole series of the boulevard from a hotel window, day and night, in all weather. The night version is the moodiest: gold lamps, blue dusk, black umbrellas. Pissarro, the oldest Impressionist, learned the city as well as the field.

exploreAction.targetName: Boulevard Montmartre at Night the gaslight
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lamps — gold pools in a blue-black evening. Pissarro painted this boulevard dozens of times from one hotel window, and the night version is the most haunting.

name: Street, Berlin
teaser: Two women in green and violet walk toward us through a crowd of angular, staring figures — a street scene that feels like a fever dream. Kirchner painted the city's energy as threat: sharp lines, clashing colors, faces like masks. The women are the fashionable 'cocottes' of Berlin's evening streets. It is Expressionism's portrait of the modern crowd, painted just before the First World War.

exploreAction.targetName: Street, Berlin the angular crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faces — angular, mask-like, staring past us. Kirchner painted Berlin's fashionable streets as a hallucination of sharp lines and electric color.

name: Black Square
teaser: A black square on a white ground — the painting that ended painting, or began it again, depending on whom you ask. Malevich hung it high in a corner of his 1915 exhibition, the place icons hung in Russian homes: it was the new icon of a new art. He called the movement Suprematism, 'the supremacy of pure feeling'. The square is not perfectly square, and the black is not uniform — up close, it breathes.

exploreAction.targetName: Black Square the icon corner
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the surface up close — cracks, brushstrokes, a black that's not flat. Malevich hung his square in the icon corner of the gallery, declaring it the sacred image of the new age.

name: White on White
teaser: A white square tilted on a white ground, edge barely visible — painting reduced to the barest possible gesture, the threshold of the visible. Malevich said the white field was 'the free void' and the square was 'the feeling of flight'. There is almost nothing there, and the nothing is the point. It is the end of the road he started with the Black Square.

exploreAction.targetName: White on White the tilted square
exploreAction.instruction: Look closely — a white square floats at an angle on a white field, held apart by the faintest edge. Malevich called it the feeling of flight, painting at the edge of nothing.

name: Reclining Nude
teaser: A woman lies on a red divan, her body stretched into a long, calm curve, her face a mask with blank eyes — Modigliani's signature nude, painted in his last, feverish years. The elongated forms echo African masks and Italian painting. The reds are warm, the pose is frank. He painted a series of these nudes; a dealer was arrested for exhibiting them in 1917, 'obscene' for showing pubic hair.

exploreAction.targetName: Reclining Nude the long curve
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the line of her body — one long, unbroken curve from head to foot. Modigliani's nudes got his dealer arrested for indecency, and they are now among the most expensive paintings ever sold.

name: Portrait of Chaim Soutine
teaser: The painter Chaim Soutine, face tilted, eyes mismatched, caught in Modigliani's angular, tender style — a portrait of a friend by a friend. The two artists lived in the same Paris slum, poor and painting. Modigliani elongated Soutine's features into elegance. Soutine survived him by decades; Modigliani died at 35. This canvas is a record of their strange, intense friendship.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of Chaim Soutine the tilted face
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eyes — one higher than the other, the face pushed into grace. Modigliani painted his poor friend Soutine in the same Montparnasse slum where both were starving artists.

name: I and the Village
teaser: A green-faced man meets a green cow face to face, their eyes linked by a thread, the village floating behind them — Chagall's dream of his Russian hometown, painted in Paris. Everything is memory made visible: the fiddler, the lovers, the upside-down house. Chagall said he painted 'not the village, but the village in me'. The cow and the man share one gaze, and the geometry is a lattice of love.

exploreAction.targetName: I and the Village the shared eye
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the thread between the man's eye and the cow's eye — a conversation across species and memory. Chagall painted his hometown from Paris, from memory, from love.

name: The Birthday
teaser: A man floats upside-down over a woman to kiss her, his head twisted to meet her lips — the most famous kiss in modern art, painted the day after Chagall's future wife's birthday. It is literally his life: the man is Chagall, the woman is Bella, and he was so happy he painted himself floating. The red room, the floating couple: love as weightlessness.

exploreAction.targetName: The Birthday the floating kiss
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the man — upside down, weightless, bending backward to kiss her. Chagall painted himself floating the day after Bella's birthday because that's what love felt like.

name: The Harlequin's Carnival
teaser: A room explodes with dancers, ladders, fish, a ladder-eyed creature and a cat playing a string — Miró's carnival of the unconscious, painted during the Paris 'Hunger Years'. The creatures are half-bio, half-toy, born of hallucinations from hunger. Miró said he painted from 'shock' images that surfaced from his mind. The floor is a chessboard, the air is full of music.

exploreAction.targetName: The Harlequin's Carnival the exploding room
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the floating creatures — a ladder, a fish, a cat with a string. Miró painted this while nearly starving in Paris, and his hunger poured out as carnival.

name: Blue II
teaser: A blue field with a single red dot, a black line and a few marks — one panel of Miró's Blue triptych, where he reduced his universe to a few signs. The red dot is a sun or an eye; the black line is a horizon or a hair. Miró called these 'the dream paintings', made after years of simplification. Blue, red, black: the minimum grammar of wonder.

exploreAction.targetName: Blue II the red dot
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the red dot — a sun, an eye, a heart, all at once, floating in the blue. Miró spent decades stripping his art down to a few signs, and this is the stripped-down universe.

name: The Song of Love
teaser: A classical head, a green ball and a rubber glove hang in a sunlit arcade — objects with no reason to meet, made mysterious by light. De Chirico painted the 'metaphysical' world where familiar things become strange. The glove is a plaster cast of a glove; the head is a sculpture. The long shadows and silent square are his signature. The Surrealists called him their prophet.

exploreAction.targetName: The Song of Love the floating glove
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the glove — a rubber glove cast in plaster, floating with a head and a ball. De Chirico made ordinary objects feel like omens, and the Surrealists worshipped him for it.

name: Mystery and Melancholy of a Street
teaser: A girl runs with a hoop through a sunlit street whose long shadows promise something terrible — one of the most haunting images of the 20th century. The arcades vanish into darkness; the shadow of an unseen figure stretches toward the child. De Chirico painted anxiety itself as architecture. The girl with the hoop is the smallest figure, and the painting is about what waits at the street's end.

exploreAction.targetName: Mystery and Melancholy of a Street the long shadow
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the shadow — it belongs to no one visible, stretching toward the running girl. De Chirico painted dread as empty streets and long light.

name: The Block
teaser: A Harlem street block in cut paper: brownstones, musicians, a funeral, a wedding, a bar — all the life of one block in one collage. Bearden cut photographs and papers from magazines and assembled a whole neighborhood. The windows show scenes inside the homes: a dinner, a party, a body laid out. It is a love letter to Harlem, where he grew up. The collage is over six feet long.

exploreAction.targetName: The Block the cut-paper street
exploreAction.instruction: Look into the windows — every one holds a different life: a dinner, a wake, a party, a man at a piano. Bearden built a whole Harlem block from cut paper, six feet of neighborhood.

name: Tar Beach
teaser: A girl lies on a rooftop at night watching the stars, her family around her — from Ringgold's story quilts, which are part painting, part quilt, part novel. The rooftop is 'Tar Beach', the family's summer living room in Harlem. The girl imagines flying over the George Washington Bridge. Ringgold wrote the story in the quilt's border. It became a children's book and a classic of Black American art.

exploreAction.targetName: Tar Beach the flying girl
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the border — the story is written right into the quilt, part of the artwork. Ringgold painted the Harlem rooftop where a girl dreams of flying, and made it a book too.

name: The Roses of Heliogabalus
teaser: Roman revelers are buried alive under a blizzard of rose petals, thrown by the emperor from a ceiling of flowers — a painting of luxury and doom, painted with fanatical detail. The emperor Heliogabalus actually did this, allegedly, at one of his feasts. Alma-Tadema painted every petal, every marble vein, every expression. He was the most successful painter in Victorian England, and his Romans are the ones Hollywood copies.

exploreAction.targetName: The Roses of Heliogabalus the petal storm
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the petals — thousands of them, painted one by one, burying the guests alive. Alma-Tadema painted the cruelest party in history with Victorian perfectionism.

name: The Lady of Shalott
teaser: A woman untangles herself from a boat's chain, three candles burning, her tapestry flowing into the river — the doomed lady from Tennyson's poem, setting out to die for love. Cursed to see the world only in a mirror, she looked out the window at Lancelot and the curse began. Waterhouse painted her at the moment of leaving the tower. The candles still burn; the river is waiting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lady of Shalott the untangled chain
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the candles — two are out, one burns: her life failing as she leaves the tower. Waterhouse painted Tennyson's doomed lady at the exact moment her curse begins.

name: Hylas and the Nymphs
teaser: A beautiful youth kneels at a lily pond while water nymphs rise to pull him under — the myth of Hylas, companion of Hercules, lured to his death by the naiads' beauty. The pond is black and deep; the girls are luminous. Waterhouse painted the moment before the pull, the youth already enchanted. The Pre-Raphaelites loved doomed beauty, and this is its peak.

exploreAction.targetName: Hylas and the Nymphs the pond
exploreAction.instruction: Look into the water — the nymphs float just below the surface, pale and patient. The youth kneels to drink and is already lost. Waterhouse painted enchantment as drowning.

name: Ophelia
teaser: A girl floats in a river, mouth open in song, flowers in her hands and dress, drowning in beauty — the most famous image of death in Victorian art. Millais painted the river for months outdoors, then painted the model in a bathtub to keep her warm; she caught pneumonia and her family sued. Ophelia's flowers are all symbolic: nettles for pain, daisies for innocence. The face was painted from the model Elizabeth Siddal.

exploreAction.targetName: Ophelia the floating girl
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the flowers — each one means something: daisies for innocence, roses for love, violets for faithfulness. The model posed in a heated bath and caught pneumonia; Millais finished the river first.

name: Christ in the House of His Parents
teaser: A young Jesus cuts his hand in Joseph's carpentry shop while Mary kisses the wound — a holy family shown as real working people, and it scandalized Victorian England. Dickens called Christ 'a wry-necked boy in a nightgown'. The Pre-Raphaelites wanted truth: the wood shavings, the scarred hands, the dirty feet. It is one of the most controversial paintings of the century.

exploreAction.targetName: Christ in the House of His Parents the cut hand
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the details — wood shavings, bare feet, a real workshop. Dickens hated this painting and said so loudly; the Pre-Raphaelites replied with more truth.

name: Proserpine
teaser: A woman holds a bitten pomegranate in a dark hall, her eyes full of a grief that has no end — the goddess of the underworld, who ate the fruit and was bound to Hades forever. The model was Jane Morris, the woman Rossetti loved from afar. She is the queen of shadows, and the painting is a portrait of longing. The ivy behind her is a symbol of clinging memory.

exploreAction.targetName: Proserpine the pomegranate
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fruit in her hand — one bite, and she is bound to the underworld forever. Rossetti painted the woman he loved as the queen of shadows, and the longing is the subject.

name: The Golden Stairs
teaser: A procession of maidens in gold descends a spiral staircase carrying musical instruments, none of them playing — a painting of music you cannot hear. There is no story, no destination; just the endless descent of beauty. Burne-Jones painted the faces from a single model, his favorite. The staircase is a golden ribbon in a dream. It was his most popular work.

exploreAction.targetName: The Golden Stairs the silent procession
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the instruments — viols, trumpets, harps, all silent. Burne-Jones painted a procession of maidens descending forever, music never played.

name: The Beguiling of Merlin
teaser: The sorcerer Merlin is trapped forever in a hawthorn tree by the enchantress Nimue, who reads from a book of spells — the fall of the greatest magician, painted in eerie greens. Nimue has taken Merlin's book and his power; his head is caught in the branches. Burne-Jones painted the moment the trap closes. The snake in the foreground is a symbol of deceit.

exploreAction.targetName: The Beguiling of Merlin the trapped wizard
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the branches — they hold Merlin like a cage, his head caught in the hawthorn. Burne-Jones painted the moment the enchantress steals the wizard's power forever.

name: The Seasons
teaser: Four women, each draped in a different season's flowers and light — Spring with blossoms, Summer with wheat, Autumn with grapes, Winter with bare branches — the poster art that made Mucha famous. The flowing hair, the floral crowns, the art-nouveau curves: this is the 'Mucha style' that defined an era of posters and jewelry. It was printed in huge runs and sold in Paris shops.

exploreAction.targetName: The Seasons the four women
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the four figures — same face, different season, each wrapped in her own flowers. Mucha turned the calendar into four goddesses and defined Art Nouveau.

name: Gismonda
teaser: A woman in Byzantine robes holds a palm frond, her head wrapped in a halo of mosaic — the poster that launched Mucha's career overnight in 1895. The actress Sarah Bernhardt loved it so much she gave him a five-year contract on the spot. The mosaic halo and the flower-woman behind her became his signature. Paris papered itself with it.

exploreAction.targetName: Gismonda the mosaic halo
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the halo — a ring of Byzantine mosaic behind the actress's head. Sarah Bernhardt saw the poster and signed Mucha to a five-year contract on the spot.

name: Radiant Baby
teaser: A crawling baby surrounded by radiating lines — Haring's first and most famous icon, drawn in chalk on New York subway stations and later everywhere. The baby was his symbol of innocence and possibility. The radiating lines make it a little sun, a little atom. Haring drew hundreds on blank subway ad panels, using white chalk so the authorities had to keep scrubbing them off.

exploreAction.targetName: Radiant Baby the crawling icon
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lines — rays of light around a crawling baby. Haring chalked this icon on subway ads by the hundreds, and it became the universal sign of his art.

name: Crack is Wack
teaser: A giant mural of a hand crushing a crack pipe, painted in red and blue on a Harlem handball court — Haring's anti-drug statement, made illegally and later preserved. The pipe cracks in the grip; the figures fracture like the drug. The city wanted to paint over it; the neighborhood fought to keep it. It still stands on the corner of 128th and 2nd Avenue.

exploreAction.targetName: Crack is Wack the crushing hand
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pipe — it's cracking apart in the hand's grip. Haring painted the mural illegally on a handball court, and the neighborhood fought the city to keep it. It still stands.

name: Abstraktes Bild
teaser: A wall of squeezed, scraped color — reds, yellows, blues dragged into a landscape of chance — from Richter's abstract series, made with a giant squeegee. Richter pulls the squeegee across wet paint, letting chance finish the work. He made hundreds of these; each is unique, each is a record of one gesture. They are among the most expensive abstract paintings ever sold.

exploreAction.targetName: Abstraktes Bild the scraped color
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the surface — layers of paint scraped by a giant squeegee, chance as co-author. Richter's abstractions sell for tens of millions, each one a single pulled gesture.

name: Betty
teaser: A woman seen from behind, head turned away, painted so photographically it could be a photo — except the blur. Richter painted from photographs and then blurred the surface, a smear of paint that reads as memory. The woman is Richter's daughter. It is a portrait of someone who will not turn around: intimacy at a distance.

exploreAction.targetName: Betty the turned head
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the blur — the brush dragged across the painted surface, like a memory failing. Richter's daughter posed, and he painted her like a photograph that's starting to fade.

name: The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living
teaser: A 14-foot tiger shark suspended in formaldehyde in a glass tank — the emblem of the 1990s British art boom, and one of the most talked-about artworks of the century. Hirst named it after his own idea: you can't picture your own death. The shark was caught and preserved; it began to rot and had to be replaced. Charles Saatchi paid £50,000 for it; it later sold for $12 million.

exploreAction.targetName: The Physical Impossibility the shark
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the shark — 14 feet of predator suspended in glass, dead and forever. Hirst's shark was replaced when the original rotted, and it sold for $12 million.

name: For the Love of God
teaser: A human skull cast in platinum and covered in 8,601 diamonds, with the original teeth still in the jaws — the most expensive single artwork ever made: £50 million in materials alone. Hirst bought the real skull from an 18th-century man. The diamonds are real; the teeth are real; the vanity is the subject. It is a memento mori for the age of bling.

exploreAction.targetName: For the Love of God the diamond skull
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the teeth — they're the original teeth of the real skull the work is cast from. Hirst covered a human skull in 8,601 diamonds and priced it at £50 million.

name: My Bed
teaser: An unmade bed with stained sheets, used condoms, a pair of tights, and a bottle of water — Emin's actual bed from a week she spent suicidal and didn't get up. The Turner Prize jury and the British public split over whether it was art. The sheets and the trash were real; the bed was her life. It sold for £2.5 million in 2014. It remains one of the most argued-about works of British art.

exploreAction.targetName: My Bed the unmade bed
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sheets — they're the actual sheets from a week Emin stayed in bed, unable to get up. She exhibited her own life, and Britain has argued about it for twenty-five years.

name: Perseus and Andromeda
teaser: The hero in winged sandals and the princess chained to a rock, the sea monster rising below — Burne-Jones's slow, dreamlike telling of the myth. The chain is real, the rock is a cliff, the monster is a coiled serpent. Perseus' arm is raised to strike, but nothing moves fast here; the whole painting hums with stillness before the rescue.

exploreAction.targetName: Perseus and Andromeda the coiled monster
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sea below the rock — the monster is already rising, coiled and patient. Burne-Jones painted the myth as a dream in which the rescue is still a moment away.

name: Venus at her Mirror (The Rokeby Venus)
teaser: Venus lies on a bed with her back to us, gazing into a mirror held by Cupid — the only surviving nude by Velázquez, and one of the most sensuous paintings ever made. The face in the mirror is slightly blurred, because Velázquez knew a mirror can't focus like an eye. It hung at Rokeby Park in England for a century. A suffragette slashed it in 1914 in protest.

exploreAction.targetName: Venus at her Mirror the blurred face
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the face in the mirror — softly blurred, because Velázquez painted how mirrors actually look. The only nude Velázquez ever painted was slashed by a suffragette in 1914 and carefully restored.

name: The Toilet of Venus
teaser: Venus at her dressing table surrounded by doves, pearls and cherubs — the Rococo goddess of luxury, painted for Madame de Pompadour's château. The pearls are real-weight, the silks are endless, the doves are Venus's birds. Boucher painted pleasure as the highest subject, and the king's mistress was his best customer. It is the Rococo at full tide.

exploreAction.targetName: The Toilet of Venus the pearls
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pearls and doves — Venus's symbols, arranged like a royal dressing room. Boucher painted this for Madame de Pompadour, whose taste defined an era of luxury.

name: The Glass of Wine
teaser: A young woman accepts a glass of wine from a cavalier who leans over her, light falling through the leaded window — a courtship scene where the meaning is in the body language. The man's hat casts a shadow; the woman's hand hesitates. The map on the wall and the music on the chair set the scene. Vermeer painted the moment the invitation is made.

exploreAction.targetName: The Glass of Wine the leaning cavalier
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the posture — he leans in, she hesitates, the wine is already poured. Vermeer painted courtship as a quiet negotiation of light and manners.

name: The Wine Glass
teaser: A seated woman with a wine glass while a man stands behind her, and a lute lies on the chair — one of Vermeer's several paintings of drinking and courtship in a sunlit room. The stained window is leaded with the Temperance figure, an ironic comment. The man's hand rests on the chair; the woman's glass is half-empty. Vermeer's light makes the moral ambiguity glow.

exploreAction.targetName: The Wine Glass the temperance window
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the window — the stained-glass figure is Temperance, watching a drinking scene. Vermeer's rooms are full of such quiet jokes.

name: The Guitar Player
teaser: A girl in a yellow jacket and ermine-trimmed hat plucks a guitar, mouth slightly open in song — Vermeer's most cheerful painting, with the sitter smiling. Music was a courtship language, and the guitar was the informal instrument of the day. The Turkish carpet, the wall map: his usual props, but the mood is looser. The girl looks like she's about to laugh at us.

exploreAction.targetName: The Guitar Player the open mouth
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her mouth — she's mid-note, singing to her own strumming. Vermeer's sitters are usually solemn; this one is having fun, and so is the painting.

name: The Concert
teaser: Three figures make music by a sunlit window: a woman at a harpsichord, a man with a lute, a woman singing from a sheet — a painting of harmony, stolen in 1990. The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum heist took this canvas, and it has never been found. The viola da gamba on the floor is part of the ensemble. It is one of the most famous missing paintings in the world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Concert the stolen canvas
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the empty chair — the second singer's place. Vermeer's Concert was stolen in the 1990 Gardner Museum heist, and its empty frame still hangs there, waiting for it.

name: The Rape of Europa
teaser: Zeus, disguised as a white bull, swims away with the princess Europa on his back while her friends wave from the shore — the god's abduction painted as a scene of sunset panic. Titian painted it for King Philip II of Spain, one of his 'poesie' series. The bull is impossibly smooth; the sky is molten. The painting crossed the Atlantic with Henry James's imagination; it hangs in Boston.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rape of Europa the swimming bull
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the bull — too white, too calm, not a real animal. Titian painted Zeus's disguise and Europa's horror at once, and the sunset is the god's own glow.

name: Diana and Callisto
teaser: The goddess Diana discovers her nymph Callisto is pregnant, and the huntress's anger freezes the forest — one of Titian's 'poesie' paintings for Philip II. The nymphs pull Callisto's clothes to reveal her secret; the goddess's pose is a storm about to break. The landscape is Arcadia gone wrong. Titian painted the myth as a study of shame and power.

exploreAction.targetName: Diana and Callisto the discovery
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Diana's posture — calm above, fury about to fall. Titian painted the moment a goddess's mercy becomes a sentence, in a forest of perfect green.

name: The Toilette of Venus
teaser: Venus at her toilet with her back to us, a mirror held by two cupids, pearls and veils everywhere — the ancestor of every 'Venus at her mirror' painting that followed. The face in the mirror is the only view of her front. Titian painted the goddess of love as a real woman in a real room. The painting's texture — the fur, the pearls, the skin — is his late style at its richest.

exploreAction.targetName: The Toilette of Venus the cupids' mirror
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mirror — held by cupids, showing the face the goddess keeps turned away. Titian's Venus set the template every later painter of the theme would copy.

name: Venus and Adonis
teaser: Venus clutches at Adonis as his hounds strain to leave for the hunt — she knows he will die, and he goes anyway. Titian painted it for Philip II, who wanted a Venus to match the Danaë. The goddess is all soft flesh; the hunter is all motion. It is the moment before tragedy, held forever. The composition was so admired that Titian painted several versions.

exploreAction.targetName: Venus and Adonis the straining hounds
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the hounds — they pull toward the hunt, and Venus holds the hunter back. Titian painted the moment before Adonis's death, and the canvas has held it for 470 years.

name: The Judgement of Paris
teaser: Three goddesses display themselves before the shepherd Paris, who must choose the fairest — the beauty contest that started the Trojan War. Rubens painted his favorite full-bodied nudes; the apple of discord is already in Paris's hand. Minerva, Juno and Venus each angle for the prize. The landscape is a golden Arcadia, and the decision will burn Troy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Judgement of Paris the three goddesses
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the three figures — each goddess is selling herself with a different strategy. Rubens painted the beauty contest that launched the Trojan War, and the apple is already in Paris's hand.

name: The Triumph of Bacchus
teaser: Bacchus crowns a soldier with ivy while a group of drinkers toast him — the god of wine as a young man in a Spanish tavern, painted with total realism. Velázquez put a classical god in a workingman's bar. The faces are real Spanish types; the wine is real wine. It is myth brought down to earth, and it scandalized and delighted Madrid in equal measure.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of Bacchus the tavern god
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faces — real drinkers, real grins, a real tavern. Velázquez brought the god of wine down from Olympus and sat him in a Spanish bar.

name: The Triumph of Galatea
teaser: The sea nymph Galatea stands on a shell drawn by dolphins, surrounded by tritons and cupids, her body spiraling with joy — Raphael's hymn to the sea and to love. The fresco was made for a banker's villa in Rome. Galatea's face is based on a real woman, the baker's daughter who was the artist's model. The colors are fresher than the myth: sea-green, gold, shell-pink.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of Galatea the spiral pose
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Galatea's body — it twists in a spiral, the whole composition whirling with her. Raphael painted the nymph's joy in a fresco that has glowed on a Roman wall for five centuries.

name: The Battle of Alexander at Issus
teaser: Two armies collide beneath a sky that is a map of the cosmos — the sun, the moon and the stars all watching the battle. Altdorfer painted the 333 BC battle of Issus as a landscape of the world: Europe on one side, Asia on the other, the Mediterranean curling between. The clouds are inscribed with the battle's date. It is the first great painting of the world seen from above.

exploreAction.targetName: The Battle of Alexander at Issus the cosmic sky
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky — the sun, moon and stars are painted into it, and the date of the battle is written in the clouds. Altdorfer painted the whole world witnessing one battle.

name: The Hunt in the Forest
teaser: Horsemen and hounds vanish into a dark forest of vertical trunks, the hunt scattering into the trees — one of the most mysterious paintings of the Renaissance. Uccello, obsessed with perspective, painted the trees receding with mathematical exactness. The dark forest swallows the riders one by one. No one knows who the hunters are or what they chase; the painting keeps its secret.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hunt in the Forest the dark trees
exploreAction.instruction: Look into the trees — each one recedes with perfect perspective, and the riders are swallowed one by one. Uccello's mathematical forest is a mystery that still has no answer.

name: The Ideal City
teaser: A perfect empty city: palaces, a triumphal arch, a temple, not a single person — the Renaissance dream of architecture as utopia. The painting is a treatise in perspective: every building recedes to a single vanishing point. The emptiness is the point; the city is the ideal, unsullied by life. It was probably a panel in a study, a vision to think about.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ideal City the empty square
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the emptiness — a perfect city with no one in it. The Renaissance painted its own dream of order, every arch and temple aligned to a single vanishing point.

name: Saint George and the Dragon
teaser: The saint on a rearing white horse drives his lance into a dragon while the princess watches from a cliff — the classic rescue, painted when Raphael was barely twenty. The horse is pure energy, the dragon is coiled pain, the background is a dream of castles and sea. Raphael painted several versions; this one is the most theatrical. It was a gift for the court of Urbino.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint George and the Dragon the rearing horse
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the horse — rearing, eyes wild, the whole rescue balanced on its hind legs. Raphael painted this at twenty, and the chivalry is already fully formed.

name: Saint Jerome in His Study
teaser: A saint reads in a palace of books, his lion sleeping on the tile floor, light falling through leaded windows — one of the first great interiors in European painting. The shelves hold real books, the tiles recede with perspective, the light is true. The lion is tame; the saint is absorbed. Antonello brought Flemish oil technique to Italy and changed everything.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint Jerome in His Study the book palace
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light — falling through the windows onto the tiles, the books, the sleeping lion. Antonello da Messina brought oil painting south, and the Renaissance learned to glow.

name: Saint Francis in Ecstasy
teaser: Saint Francis stands on a rocky ledge, arms spread, receiving the stigmata in a landscape that glows with dawn — the saint and the earth both transfigured. The light is God's, and it falls on the rocks, the donkey, the shepherd. Bellini painted the miracle as a sunrise. The desert behind Francis is painted with the precision of a naturalist.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint Francis in Ecstasy the glowing dawn
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light — it falls on Francis and on every rock and leaf around him. Bellini painted the miracle as a sunrise over a landscape that itself seems to be praying.

name: The Deposition from the Cross
teaser: The dead Christ is lowered from the cross while the mourners around him weep in unison — a composition of grief arranged like a frieze, each face a different register of sorrow. The bodies curve in one continuous line of loss. Mary faints, the Magdalene twists her hands, the disciples hold the body. It is the most influential painting of the Northern Renaissance.

exploreAction.targetName: The Deposition from the Cross the falling body
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the line of bodies — the whole painting curves like a wave of grief, Mary fainting at the left, the Magdalene weeping at the right. Van der Weyden made sorrow itself a composition.

name: The Crucifixion
teaser: Christ on the cross between the Virgin and Saint John, their faces wet with tears, the sky gold — a Crucifixion reduced to its essential witnesses. Van der Weyden compressed the scene to three figures and the cross, and made the emotion the subject. The gold background is timeless, not natural; the grief is entirely natural. It is one of the most moving paintings of the 15th century.

exploreAction.targetName: The Crucifixion the three witnesses
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the faces — the Virgin and John are crying, painted with a realism that shocked viewers in 1440. Van der Weyden made grief the center of the crucifixion.

name: The Pilgrims of Emmaus
teaser: Two disciples at a table recognize the risen Christ as he breaks bread — the moment of recognition, painted so vividly the fruit on the table seems to roll. The younger disciple's arms fly open; the older one grips the chair. Caravaggio painted the everyday meal turning sacred. The shell on the pilgrim's cloak marks him as a traveler; the light marks the stranger as God.

exploreAction.targetName: The Pilgrims of Emmaus the breaking bread
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the disciple's arms — thrown wide in shock as he recognizes the stranger. Caravaggio painted the sacred moment as a tavern meal, and the table still seems to tremble.

name: The Death of the Virgin
teaser: The Virgin lies dead in a bare room, her body swollen and unidealized, the apostles grieving around her — a painting so honest it was rejected by the church that commissioned it. Caravaggio used a real drowned woman as his model, and the monks called the result 'not decent'. The bare feet, the plain dress, the raw grief: he painted death as it is. It now hangs in the Louvre.

exploreAction.targetName: The Death of the Virgin the bare feet
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Virgin's body — ordinary, unidealized, the body of a real dead woman. Caravaggio modeled her on a drowned woman, and the church rejected the painting as indecent.

name: The Flagellation
teaser: Christ is tied to a column while three men take turns whipping him, the light brutal and exact — Caravaggio's realism at its most direct. The torturers are ordinary men doing a job; the column is a real column. The light falls across the bodies like a spotlight. It was painted for a church in Naples, and the violence is unflinching. There are two versions; the Naples one is the original.

exploreAction.targetName: The Flagellation the three whips
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the torturers — ordinary men, leaning into their work. Caravaggio's realism made the passion of Christ feel like an event you could walk into.

name: The Road to Calvary
teaser: A crowd surges toward the cross, Christ at its center, nearly lost in the crush — the procession to the crucifixion painted as a river of bodies. Tintoretto's diagonal composition pushes everything toward the upper right, the cross already waiting. The crowd is enormous, pressing, indifferent. Christ is barely visible in the middle of it, which is the point: he is being carried along by events.

exploreAction.targetName: The Road to Calvary the crush
exploreAction.instruction: Look for Christ — almost hidden in the crowd, carried along like a leaf. Tintoretto painted the passion as a mass of people pushing toward an event too big for any of them.

name: John the Baptist
teaser: The Baptist emerges from darkness, one finger pointing upward, a mysterious smile on his lips — a painting that seems to glow from within. The finger points to heaven; the smile is the Mona Lisa's cousin. The animal-skin robe and the reed cross mark him as the desert prophet. Leonardo painted him in his last years, in the smoky style he perfected. The darkness around him is almost tactile.

exploreAction.targetName: John the Baptist the pointing finger
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the finger — pointing up, out of the darkness, toward something we can't see. Leonardo's Baptist smiles like he knows the secret the painting is pointing at.

name: The Musicians
teaser: Four young men make music by candlelight, one tuning a lute, one blowing a horn, one with his head tilted — painted for Caravaggio's first patron, Cardinal del Monte. The boys are real street musicians, painted with warm realism. The second figure is thought to be Caravaggio himself. The sheet music in the front is a madrigal about love, painted so accurately it could be read.

exploreAction.targetName: The Musicians the candlelight
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the second figure tuning his lute — likely Caravaggio's own face. The cardinal who bought it loved music, and Caravaggio painted him a concert in candlelight.

name: The Lute Player
teaser: A boy in a loose white shirt plays a lute, eyes half-closed in the music, flowers and fruit on the table before him — Caravaggio's most sensuous early work. The boy is probably a castrato singer in Cardinal del Monte's household. The music is real, the flowers are wilting, the light is amber. The painting has been stolen twice and recovered both times, most recently in 1997 after a decade missing.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lute Player the half-closed eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eyes — half-closed, the boy lost in the music. The lute player was stolen in 1969 and only recovered in 1997, hidden in a Ukrainian monastery.

name: The Young Bacchus
teaser: The wine god lounges with a glass of dark wine, grapes and vine leaves in his hair, offering us the cup — a self-portrait in disguise. The boy holding the wine is Caravaggio's friend, the painter Mario Minniti, who modeled for many early works. The fruit is rotting at the edges — Caravaggio painted decay inside the celebration. The god of wine looks tired, like he's been up all night.

exploreAction.targetName: The Young Bacchus the offered cup
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fruit — already rotting at the edges. Caravaggio painted the god of wine with decay creeping in, a celebration that knows it will end.

name: Medusa
teaser: The severed head of Medusa screams from a convex shield, snakes writhing — Caravaggio painted it on a real parade shield, so the face distorts as if reflected in a mirror. The artist painted his own face as the Gorgon, mouth open in terror. It was a gift to the Medici family, whose emblem was Medusa's head. The shield was carried in processions; the horror was meant to repel.

exploreAction.targetName: Medusa the screaming shield
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the distortion — the face warps because it's painted on a real convex shield. Caravaggio used his own face for the Gorgon, and the Medici carried it in parades.

name: Head of Medusa
teaser: The severed Gorgon head, snakes hissing from the neck, blood still fresh — Rubens's answer to Caravaggio's Medusa, painted with Baroque muscle. The snakes are individual portraits, each one coiled and venomous. The eyes are wide, the mouth open in a final scream. Rubens painted it as a study of horror, and the horror is vivid enough to look away from. It hangs in Vienna.

exploreAction.targetName: Head of Medusa the hissing snakes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the snakes — each one painted as a separate, hissing creature. Rubens turned the Gorgon's severed head into a study of pure horror, and it works.

name: Salome
teaser: Salome holds the platter with the Baptist's head while an old woman stares and the executioner looks away — a painting about the weight of a severed head. The head on the platter is Caravaggio's own face again. The executioner is looking at us, not at what he's done. The gold, the dark, the silence: it's a scene from a nightmare that refuses to wake.

exploreAction.targetName: Salome the platter
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the head on the platter — Caravaggio's face yet again, painted while he was on the run for murder. The executioner meets our eyes; nobody looks at the head.

name: Saint Catherine of Alexandria
teaser: The virgin martyr leans on her wheel, the palm of martyrdom in her hand, her face patient and proud — Caravaggio painted her as a real Roman woman, not a saint. The wheel is the instrument of her torture, broken by angels. The sword is the one that killed her. She looks at us like she's waiting for the question. The saint was modeled on a courtesan, which scandalized the church.

exploreAction.targetName: Saint Catherine the wheel
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the wheel — the instrument of her torture, already broken. Caravaggio's saint was modeled on a courtesan, and the church complained about the model more than the martyrdom.

name: Mary Magdalene in Ecstasy
teaser: The Magdalene leans back with eyes closed, mouth open, lost in a rapture that looks like abandon — one of the most sensual religious paintings ever made. The saint is shown at the moment of mystical union, but the pose is a lover's. The painting disappeared for centuries and was only rediscovered in 2014 in a private collection. It remains one of the most controversial works of the Baroque.

exploreAction.targetName: Mary Magdalene in Ecstasy the closed eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pose — ecstasy that looks like surrender. Caravaggio's Magdalene disappeared for centuries and surfaced in 2014 in a private collection, still scandalous.

name: The Crucifixion of Saint Andrew
teaser: The apostle is nailed to an X-shaped cross, his executioners straining to raise it, the old man's face calm amid the labor — Caravaggio's last known painting, finished in 1610, the year he died. The saint chose the diagonal cross because he was unworthy to die like Christ. The executioners are exhausted; the saint is at peace. It was painted in Naples while Caravaggio was a fugitive, and it survives as his final word.

exploreAction.targetName: The Crucifixion of Saint Andrew the x cross
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the saint's face — calm, while the men around him strain and sweat. Caravaggio's last painting, finished the year he died, shows a man choosing his own death with dignity.

name: The Raising of Lazarus
teaser: Christ commands the dead man to rise, and Lazarus sits up, halfway between death and life, while the crowd recoils — painted on the run in Sicily, using his own exhausted face for Lazarus. The outstretched arm of Christ and the rising arm of Lazarus nearly touch. The painting was cut down and damaged over centuries, but the power survives. Caravaggio painted the threshold of death from the inside.

exploreAction.targetName: The Raising of Lazarus the reaching arms
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two arms — Christ's commanding, Lazarus's rising, almost meeting. Caravaggio used his own face for the risen man, a fugitive painting himself back from the dead.

name: The Ascension
teaser: Christ rises into a burst of golden light while the apostles below reach up from darkness — one of Rembrandt's Passion series for the Prince of Orange. The light is the event: a column of gold tearing the darkness. The apostles are small, dazzled, arms out. Rembrandt painted the miracle as a physical fact of light and shadow. It is one of the few ascensions that feels like it's really happening.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ascension the golden column
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light — a column of gold that seems to lift Christ by itself. Rembrandt painted the ascension as a physical event, and the apostles below are blinded by it.

name: The Assumption
teaser: The Virgin rises through rings of angels into a golden heaven while the apostles stare up in wonder — the painting that made Titian famous at 28, hung over the altar of Venice's greatest church. The red and blue of her robe are the anchors; the gold above is pure light. It is one of the largest altarpieces in Italy. Titian's triumph at the Frari church announced the Venetian Renaissance.

exploreAction.targetName: The Assumption the rising virgin
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the rising figure — the red robe and blue cloak floating into gold. Titian was 28 when this made him the most famous painter in Venice.

name: The Immaculate Conception
teaser: The Virgin floats on a crescent moon among clouds and cherubs, hands folded, wrapped in blue and white — the definitive image of a doctrine, painted so often by Murillo it became the standard. The crescent moon, the stars, the crushed serpent: every symbol of the Immaculate Conception is here. Seville's churches filled with his versions. It is the most reproduced Spanish religious image of its time.

exploreAction.targetName: The Immaculate Conception the crescent moon
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the moon under her feet — the classic symbol of the Immaculate Conception, painted by the artist who defined the image for all of Spain.

name: The Visitation
teaser: Two pregnant women embrace — Mary and Elizabeth, both expecting, both glowing — painted with Pontormo's strange, luminous palette of pink, green and blue. The figures are elongated, the colors are not natural, the emotion is enormous. The women lean in at the same angle, mirroring each other. It is Mannerism's most tender painting, and one of its strangest.

exploreAction.targetName: The Visitation the two expectant women
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the colors — pink, green and blue that don't exist in nature. Pontormo painted the meeting of Mary and Elizabeth as a dance of two women who both carry miracles.

name: The Nativity
teaser: Angels dance on the roof of the stable while the infant Christ lies on the ground — a Nativity painted in the shadow of the end of the world, which Botticelli believed was imminent. He signed it with a prophecy of the Apocalypse. The angels embrace; the devils flee beneath the rocks. The joy is real and the dread is real. It was painted around 1500, the year of his fear.

exploreAction.targetName: The Nativity the dancing angels
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the angels on the roof — dancing, embracing, while devils flee into the rocks below. Botticelli signed this joyful nativity with a prophecy of the apocalypse.

name: The Presentation in the Temple
teaser: Mary presents the infant Jesus to the old priest Simeon beneath a golden canopy — a panel of quiet ceremony and jewel colors. The roundels in the frame show prophets; the gold is heaven. Fra Angelico's compositions are always calm, always clear, always warm. The Presentation was a favorite theme of his convent of San Marco, where the friars painted to pray.

exploreAction.targetName: The Presentation in the Temple the golden canopy
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the gold — heaven itself as a canopy over the ceremony. Fra Angelico painted prayer itself: calm, clear, radiant.

name: The Flight into Egypt
teaser: The Holy Family crosses a wintry landscape with an enormous blue mountainside looming — Mary rides the donkey, Joseph leads, and the world around them is Bruegel's beloved detail. The mountain is imaginary, enormous, blue; the family is tiny beneath it. Bruegel painted the flight as a landscape, and the landscape swallows the story. The snow, the village, the frozen river: the world goes on.

exploreAction.targetName: The Flight into Egypt the blue mountain
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mountain — enormous, blue, dwarfing the tiny family. Bruegel painted the holy escape as a landscape, and the world's business continues all around them.

name: The Holy Family
teaser: Mary, Joseph and the infant Christ form a dense, sculptural knot of bodies — the Doni Tondo's sibling, one of the few paintings Michelangelo finished. The bodies twist like carved marble. The infant reaches for Mary, Mary reaches toward Joseph, Joseph looks on from behind. It is the Holy Family as a study of three bodies and one bond. The paint is thick, the forms are heavy, the love is solid.

exploreAction.targetName: The Holy Family the sculptural knot
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the bodies — intertwined like carved stone. Michelangelo the sculptor painted the family as a knot of muscle and tenderness.

name: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt
teaser: The Holy Family rests in the desert at night, Joseph holding the sheet music while an angel plays the violin for the sleeping infant — a lullaby made visible. The angel is a boy with wings, playing from behind. The light is the music. It is one of Caravaggio's most tender paintings, painted in his early Roman years. The angel's back is to us, the melody goes to the child.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rest on the Flight into Egypt the violinist
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the angel — playing a violin from behind, the music flowing toward the sleeping child. Caravaggio painted a desert lullaby, and it is his gentlest masterpiece.

name: The Return from Egypt
teaser: The Holy Family walks home through a landscape of rocks and olives, the child now walking on his own — the end of the flight, painted by the painter who invented European painting. Giotto's figures have weight and faces and feelings. The return is quiet: no drama, just a family coming home. The fresco cycle it belongs to is the foundation of Renaissance art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Return from Egypt the walk home
