exploreAction.instruction: Look at the walking child — the flight is over, the family is coming home. Giotto, the first modern painter, painted the return as quietly as a family photo.

name: The Disputation of Saint Catherine
teaser: The saint argues her faith before the emperor while the pagan philosophers listen, her face alight with certainty — Correggio painted the moment a young woman out-argues an empire. The composition is a pyramid of light and attention, all eyes on Catherine. The emperor's throne tips away; the philosophers lean in. Correggio's soft light and warm color made him the most lyrical painter of the High Renaissance.

exploreAction.targetName: The Disputation of Saint Catherine the argument
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the eyes — everyone in the painting is watching Catherine, and she is radiant with the argument. Correggio painted the moment reason becomes light.

name: The Parnassus
teaser: Apollo plays a viola da braccio on the mountain of poetry while nine muses and nine great poets listen — Homer, Sappho, Dante, Petrarch all gathered on one slope. Raphael painted it in the Vatican, filling the mountain with the poets he loved. The muses are real women; the poets are real faces. It is the Renaissance's image of poetry as the highest music.

exploreAction.targetName: The Parnassus the poets' mountain
exploreAction.instruction: Look for Homer and Sappho — the ancient poets sit beside Dante and Petrarch, all listening to Apollo. Raphael painted poetry as one continuous conversation across the centuries.

name: The Fire in the Borgo
teaser: A fire rages behind St Peter's while people flee, carry the sick, and reach down from the walls — a fresco of panic painted with perfect calm. A woman hands her child down from a wall; a naked youth climbs to safety. The pope in the distance prays, and the fire stops — the miracle the fresco records. Raphael's composition of running figures set the standard for action scenes for centuries.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fire in the Borgo the fleeing crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the mother passing her child over the wall — a gesture of panic painted with classical grace. Raphael staged the fire as an opera, and the pope's prayer ends it.

name: The Liberation of Saint Peter
teaser: An angel leads the apostle out of a torchlit prison while the guards sleep — a night scene painted in the Vatican, with light doing the storytelling. The angel's light is the only light: it floods the cell, startles the guards, and guides the escape. Raphael painted the moonlight, the torchlight and the divine light all at once. It is one of the first great night paintings in Western art.

exploreAction.targetName: The Liberation of Saint Peter the angel light
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light sources — torch, moonlight and the angel's glow all fighting the dark. Raphael's night escape scene set the template for every prison break in art.

name: The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple
teaser: A robber is trampled by a heavenly horseman in the temple, his money bags scattered — the divine police arriving mid-theft. Raphael painted the Vatican's lesson: the Church's treasure is protected by God. The robber is thrown down, the crowd parts, the priest prays. The horseman and his companions are light itself. It is one of the most dramatic frescoes in the Vatican.

exploreAction.targetName: The Expulsion of Heliodorus the divine horseman
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the fallen man — money bags scattered, trampled by a horseman made of light. Raphael painted divine justice arriving in the temple like a cavalry charge.

name: The Mass at Bolsena
teaser: A doubting priest watches the host bleed on the altar cloth at Bolsena — a miracle painted as a moment of personal conversion. The priest is the one who doubted transubstantiation, and the blood proved him wrong. The women in the foreground watch, moved; the Swiss Guard kneels in the painted crowd, a portrait of real soldiers. Raphael made a dogma into a drama.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mass at Bolsena the bleeding host
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the altar cloth — stained with blood, the miracle the priest needed. Raphael painted the real Swiss Guard into the scene, giving the dogma a documentary feel.

name: The Meeting of Leo the Great and Attila
teaser: The pope rides out to meet the Hun king, and Attila's horse rears back as the apostles Peter and Paul appear in the sky with swords — the legend of Rome saved by faith. Raphael painted the modern pope's face on Leo. The swords in the sky are the real argument; Attila turns away. It is a fresco of divine intervention, staged like a cavalry standoff.

exploreAction.targetName: The Meeting of Leo the Great and Attila the sky swords
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky — Peter and Paul descending with swords, turning the Huns' horses. Raphael painted Rome's legend of the moment faith stopped an invasion.

name: The Donation of Constantine
teaser: The emperor Constantine kneels to hand the crown of Rome to the pope — the document that justified papal power for a thousand years, painted on the Vatican's wall. The donors are the emperor's court; the recipient is the Church. The fresco celebrates the forged 'Donation of Constantine', later proved a fake. The painting outlived the document: the power was real either way.

exploreAction.targetName: The Donation of Constantine the kneeling emperor
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the kneeling emperor — handing over an empire to a priest. The document this fresco celebrates was later proved a forgery, but the power it claimed lasted a millennium.

name: The Creation of Man
teaser: God reaches from a cloud of angels and touches Adam's fingertip — the single most reproduced image in art history. Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel on his back over four years, and this panel is its heart. The space between the fingers is the painting: the spark of life itself. The figure of God is wrapped in a cloak whose shape some see as a human brain, a Renaissance nod to intellect.

exploreAction.targetName: The Creation of Man the almost-touch
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the gap between the fingers — the whole painting lives in that space. Michelangelo's ceiling took four years, and this panel became the most copied image in history.

name: The Creation of Eve
teaser: Eve rises from Adam's side while God watches, the first woman stepping into existence — one of the Sistine ceiling's central panels. The figures are monumental, sculpted in paint. Eve's hands are raised in wonder and prayer at once. Adam sleeps, God stands, Eve is born. Michelangelo compressed the whole of Genesis into nine panels, and this is its quietest miracle.

exploreAction.targetName: The Creation of Eve the rising figure
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Eve's hands — raised in wonder as she steps out of Adam's side. Michelangelo gave the first woman a gesture that is both prayer and arrival.

name: The Separation of Light from Darkness
teaser: God hurls the universe apart with both arms, light and dark tearing from his body — the first day of creation, painted as pure cosmic violence. Michelangelo's God is enormous, his robe spinning like a galaxy. It was the last panel he painted, and he painted it in one day. The power is physical: the Creator's body is the engine of the cosmos.

exploreAction.targetName: The Separation of Light from Darkness the cosmic god
exploreAction.instruction: Look at God's body — the universe tearing out of his own limbs. Michelangelo painted the first day of creation as a physical act, and finished it in a single day.

name: The Deluge
teaser: The flood waters rise while people claw onto a shrinking island, one boat already swamped — the first panel Michelangelo painted on the Sistine ceiling. The figures are a catalog of panic: a father carrying his son, a man clinging to a tree, a family under a tent. The rain falls in silver streaks. The power of the whole ceiling is here in miniature, painted before the style matured.

exploreAction.targetName: The Deluge the rising water
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the island — people climbing over each other as the water takes the last dry ground. Michelangelo's first ceiling panel is a study of panic in every register.

name: The Prophet Isaiah
teaser: The prophet sits with a book, one finger marking his place, a putto reaching up — Raphael's prophet for the church of Sant'Agostino, painted in his most sculptural style. The figure has the weight of marble and the ease of a man pausing mid-thought. The putti are pure charm. The fresco was restored to its original jewel colors in 2009.

exploreAction.targetName: The Prophet Isaiah the marking finger
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the finger in the book — a scholar interrupted by inspiration. Raphael gave the prophet the body of a god and the habit of a reader.

name: The Prophet Jeremiah
teaser: The weeping prophet sits in shadow, head bowed, one hand on his chin — the gloomiest figure on the Sistine ceiling, and the one that looks most like Michelangelo himself. Jeremiah wrote the book of Lamentations, and his pose is grief itself. The other prophets gesture and prophesy; Jeremiah just sits, bowed, knowing. It is often read as the artist's self-portrait of his own melancholy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Prophet Jeremiah the bowed head
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the pose — a man folded into his own grief, chin in hand. Michelangelo's Jeremiah is the prophet of sorrow, and his face is often read as the artist's own.

name: The Cumaean Sibyl
teaser: An aged prophetess with enormous forearms turns the pages of a book of destiny — one of the five sibyls on the Sistine ceiling, women who prophesied Christ before he came. The Cumaean Sibyl was the one who guided Aeneas to the underworld and asked to live a thousand years. Michelangelo gave her a body that has done exactly that. The muscles are the age; the gaze is the prophecy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cumaean Sibyl the turning pages
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the arms — aged, powerful, the body of a woman who asked for a thousand years. Michelangelo's sibyls are the strongest figures on the ceiling.

name: The Delphic Sibyl
teaser: The youngest and most beautiful of the sibyls turns toward us, scroll in hand, eyes wide as if she just heard the prophecy — the most graceful figure on the Sistine ceiling. Her hair is braided like a crown, her colors are green and gold. The Delphic sibyl was the oracle of Apollo; Michelangelo made her the face of revelation itself. She is the ceiling's most reproduced face after Adam.

exploreAction.targetName: The Delphic Sibyl the wide eyes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at her eyes — wide, as if the prophecy is arriving as we watch. Michelangelo's Delphic Sibyl is the ceiling's most beautiful figure and its most alert.

name: The Libyan Sibyl
teaser: A prophetess twists to lift a heavy book from a shelf behind her, every muscle in her back visible — one of the most anatomically astonishing figures ever painted. Michelangelo's sibyl is a contortionist of prophecy. The twist of the torso is a tour de force of drawing. The faces on the ceiling were repainted in the 1980s restoration, and the Libyan Sibyl emerged from the soot as a woman of coral and gold.

exploreAction.targetName: The Libyan Sibyl the twisted back
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the back — the twist of the torso is pure anatomy, a figure drawn from every angle at once. The restoration revealed her in coral and gold after centuries of soot.

name: The Ignudi
teaser: Twenty naked young men sit in the corners of the Sistine ceiling, holding ribbons and acorns, framing the Genesis scenes — the most famous supporting cast in art history. The 'ignudi' have no story; they are pure body, painted as studies of the human form in every pose. Each one is a different exercise in anatomy. Michelangelo's nudes became the standard against which all figure drawing was measured for centuries.

exploreAction.targetName: The Ignudi the twenty nudes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the poses — twenty young men, each a different study of the body in space. Michelangelo painted them with no story at all, only anatomy, and they became the school of European art.

name: The Drunkenness of Noah
teaser: Noah lies naked and drunk while his sons cover him with a cloth, one son mocking, two looking away — the first panel of the Sistine ceiling, painted before Michelangelo found his style. The shame of the patriarch is shown without judgment. The sons' gestures set the pattern: Shem and Japheth walk backward to cover him, Ham points and laughs. It is a family story told with the weight of tragedy.

exploreAction.targetName: The Drunkenness of Noah the covering cloth
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the three sons — one mocks, two look away, all of them handling their father's shame differently. Michelangelo began the ceiling with this human, undivine scene.

name: The Sacrifice of Noah
teaser: Noah and his family build an altar and offer a sacrifice of thanks after the flood, the smoke rising toward a God we don't see — one of the Sistine ceiling's panels, painted with the family in vivid domestic motion. The carcass is carried, the fire is lit, the smoke curls. Michelangelo's God is off-frame; the human world does the work. The panel was damaged in the 1790s by an exploding gunpowder store.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sacrifice of Noah the rising smoke
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the family — carrying the carcass, tending the fire, doing the work of thanks. Michelangelo painted the human side of the covenant; God is off the ceiling, unseen.

name: The Brazen Serpent
teaser: A bronze snake coils around a pole while the Israelites bitten by serpents writhe at its base — the Sistine ceiling's most violent panel, painted with bodies in every state of suffering. The ones who look at the bronze serpent are healed; the ones who don't are dying. Michelangelo turned a biblical remedy into a knot of agony and hope. The contortions are his study of the body under extremes.

exploreAction.targetName: The Brazen Serpent the coiled snake
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the base of the pole — bodies twisting, bitten, dying, while the healed look up. Michelangelo painted the cure and the disease in one continuous coil.

name: David and Goliath
teaser: The giant Goliath crumples at the bottom of the scene while the boy David, half his size, stands over him — one of the corner spandrels of the Sistine ceiling, painted as a study of David's impossible win. Michelangelo compressed the whole fight into one image: the sling, the fall, the victory. The two bodies form a cross shape. It is the underdog story painted at the scale of a ceiling.

exploreAction.targetName: David and Goliath the crumpled giant
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the scale — the giant is down, the boy is standing, the sling is still in his hand. Michelangelo made the whole battle one image in the corner of his ceiling.
